utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Registrar, will you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Good afternoon, everyone in and around the courtroom. This is case number IT-04-74-T, the Prosecutor versus Prlic et al. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Registrar. Today is Monday, 13th of July. Good afternoon to you, Mr. Praljak, to you, Mr. Prlic, Mr. Stojic, Mr. Petkovic, and Mr. Pusic. Of course, my thoughts go out to Mr. Coric. Good afternoon to the Defence counsel, to you, Mr. Stringer, and all your associates, and good afternoon to all the people assisting us. Mr. Kovacic, you wanted to have the floor?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I apologise for taking up your time. I will be brief, however. The OTP last week again informed us that documents that they intend to do in their cross-examination will be provided to us piecemeal, in batches. I read what the Prosecutor said on the 9th of June, 2009, and what was said can be interpreted in various ways, and that's why I did not react on the day, on the 9th, when that was last discussed. In any case, now I believe that it should be noted that so far in the case, in keeping with your instructions that have been in place from day 1, the party conducting cross-examination has always informed the other party about documents by submitting the list of documents, so they always informed about the documents that will be used in cross-examination. Last week, we received a binder, and the Prosecutor also informed us that the next binder would follow. We appreciate all the technical difficulties, but in any case we believe that the Defence is entitled to receive a complete list of documents, if, for nothing else, than to provide us with an opportunity to be more efficient. We have to look at the documents for technical reasons. They may be wrongly translated, they don't have to be authentic, which is all the things that we can check before the documents appear in the courtroom. In other words, we can object in due course; for example, when there are some pages lacking or when the translation was erroneous. Therefore, I would kindly ask that -- the OTP to provide the Defence as soon as possible with the list of documents that they intend to use during their cross-examination. Obviously, we are aware of the fact that that list may be supplemented or subtracted. That has always been the case so far. We are not requiring 100 per cent accuracy, but we are looking for goodwill on the part of the OTP, and we would like them to disclose the documents as soon as possible, just like we did when it was our turn to cross-examine during the Prosecution case. I would like to remind everybody that the Defence has given up the right to contact the accused during his testimony in order to maintain his credibility, but that doesn't mean that we don't -- we are willing to give up on the chance to look at the document and see, well in advance, whether there are grounds to object on technical merit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Do you have anything to say, Mr. Stringer?

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. Good afternoon. Good afternoon, Your Honours, Counsel, and everyone else around the courtroom. I don't see what purpose it would really serve, given the unique circumstances that we have here with the witness who's been testifying for ten weeks. We're four days away from going into a four-week recess, and I can assure the Trial Chamber that I'm going to use that four weeks to continue to prepare the cross-examination, based upon the very extensive testimony that's been given to date. Now, I appreciate or I understand that counsel's indicating that there won't be any communication with the general over the course of the recess, at least not about what the cross-examination documents will be, but what we've proposed, I think, is entirely sensible and, I think, is a good reflection of, in fact, how we can work more efficiently during this time. We've got another binder ready today that is going to take us into the next phase probably through the rest of the week. We don't have any more binders prepared because, to be honest, Mr. President, I'm not sure exactly where I'm going to go with this when we come back from the recess. And I'm not under any obligation at this point to tell anyone where I am going. I can give Mr. Kovacic a list of potential exhibits. It will probably have about 2500 documents on it. I'm not going to provide those to him in hard copy at this point because I'm not going to ask my staff to go through the tremendous and wasteful effort of putting binders together that are filled with papers that may or may not be used during a cross-examination that is going to probably extend through the end of September. So it's just highly inefficient to do anything, I would suggest, than what we're doing now, which is to provide all the parties in advance. Mr. Kovacic has had the current binder over the weekend. He can see what the documents are going to be for today or tomorrow. We've got the next one available. They're in the order that the witness is going to be presented with them, which I think -- or based upon past experience is everyone's strong preference, rather than trying to move around a large number of binders. So, I -- well, let me just briefly sort of reset what makes this unique. First of all, this is an accused for whom the Trial Chamber and the Appeals Chamber has ruled that all communications can continue throughout the time that the witness is testifying, even while he's testifying on cross-examination, which makes this situation completely unique compared to any of the other witnesses who've appeared previously in this trial. And I appreciate counsel's statements about sort of a voluntary arrangement they've made not to talk about cross-examination, but there isn't really anything binding about that or there isn't anything that could prevent that from changing. We view cross-examination and the ability to put a witness -- put a document in front of the witness, under these circumstances, we view that as being an essential component of cross-examination, and when you've got a witness who's going to be testifying on cross for a few days, which has always been the case in this trial, then, of course, the procedure that we've always had is one that works for everybody. The binder are given to the witness, they're distributed to everyone. No one has contact -- no one's permitted to have contact with the witness at that time because the witness is under oath, and of course the documents in the cross-examination will be completed in, say, four hours of court time, maybe more for a few witnesses, but of course that situation isn't anything like what we have here, where all communications are permissible, the examination won't be finished until possibly late September - I don't know - and it provides, in our view, a very strong potential to undermine what for the Prosecution is our right to an effective cross-examination, and that is effectiveness being very largely based upon the documents and the way they're presented to the witnesses on cross-examination, as has been the case throughout this trial and also for the other Defence teams. So that's our response. It's -- we're going to go to recess at the end of this week. We've got all the documents ready to get us through the week. We're going to be distributing those shortly. I can't -- I don't have anything that is remotely as final, in terms of the documents that we're going to be getting into six weeks from now or four weeks from now, five weeks from now. That's all going to happen over the break. So as I said, if Mr. Kovacic wants to have a big list of documents that we might potentially use, and of course I'll include -- you know, I'll go -- I'll be very careful and include documents on there that I might use so that I won't have any difficulties later, but I just think it's -- I don't -- if I could suggest, I think that's not what he wants, frankly, but that's all I can give him at this point. And if that's what he wants, we can, I suppose, give it. But I think, Mr. President, that the much more efficient and fair procedure is the one that we're following here, which is to distribute binders as we get to the topics. Everyone will have them sufficiently far in advance to go through them and look to see if there are any translation issues, et cetera, which I think generally doesn't happen until we're actually all looking at the document. But, in any event, that's my response, Mr. President, and I think that we've come up, under these unique circumstances, with a situation that is the best and most efficient, and this is how we intend to proceed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Stringer, last time you told us that you were going to address topics by topics. When are we going to have this list of topics; in the next few days, or are you planning to wait until we resume on the 17th of August to give us the list? And, secondly, are we going to finish with this binder for this week and then you have a second binder for this week; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. Just to take your last question first, we've got another binder here, and we can distribute that whenever. It's ready to go. In response to your first question, I hadn't intended to actually distribute a list of the topics, itself. The documents or the binders are arranged by topic, and as you pointed out last week, Mr. President, the current set of documents relates to what we generally are calling or thinking of as credibility issues based upon prior testimony of the witness. The next set of documents will relate generally to the issue of international armed conflict. I think that will be pretty obvious once we start going through those documents. And then after that, you know, we'll get to JCE and the various crime bases, et cetera, after the break. So I hadn't intended on distributing a specific list of the topics; rather, the binders of the documents will be assembled according to -- or they'll be separated by topic, if I can put it that way. I could provide you with a list of topics, Mr. President. Again, at this stage, because I'm probably going to be doing a lot of retooling over the summer break, the list I give you today might not necessarily resemble the one that I would be working with when we commence again in mid-August.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I will not tackle all the arguments that we've just heard. We're glad that the OTP has provided us with some more details vis-a-vis their position. However, I would like to deal with two positions on the part of the OTP. First of all, the fact is that the Prosecutor has heard the entire testimony, he was listening to it continuously, so the cross could have been prepared in the same continuous manner. Therefore, I would not agree with the claim that the OTP prepares their cross-examination from the moment when the accused finishes examination-in-chief. I fully believe that that activity should have already been taking place in parallel with the examination-in-chief. And in addition to that, the Prosecutor knew what would happen. He knew that General Praljak's testimony will take some time. And also the Prosecutor knew at the time that the Trial Chamber, two months prior to the beginning of Mr. Praljak's testimony, issued a decision allowing the Defence to communicate with the accused during his testimony. Therefore, all the elements that might serve the OTP to make a decision as to how to prepare the cross-examination were well known before the testimony and during the testimony itself. And just one more argument that I would like to deal with. If the Prosecutor thinks that it is all right to provide the Trial Chamber and the Defence teams with a list of documents which is incomplete and which is provided batch by batch, then I would like to follow up on Judge Antonetti's words or, rather, his question about the list of topics, and I would like to remind you of the way my learned friend Alaburic did things. Ms. Alaburic prepared quite a lengthy cross-examination, and that's why she prepared a different method of preparation, and she duly informed everybody in the courtroom, the Trial Chamber and the Defence counsel, how she wished to proceed. I remind you that she provided us with a list of topics and the documents accompanying every topic. The proposal on the part of the Prosecutor, to provide us with a large, rough list, I don't think this is at all useful because this is a list of documents that have been disclosed so far and he can use any of them. He has to be more specific than that. I believe that we can agree that the list should follow in blocks, although based on the hitherto practice I believe that the list of documents that will be used should be disclosed at the beginning of the cross-examination. If the Trial Chamber is of the opinion that the Prosecution should be given an opportunity to do it in batches because of the scope of the cross-examination, still we believe that they should provide us with the topics and the list of documents accompanying that particular topic before they start dealing with the particular topic. And I would like to underline one more thing. The Prosecutor was well aware of the situation and had all the elements in place when Praljak started testifying. He knew everything, the rules of the game were known, so he should not have taken the risk of waiting for another kind of solution that would make the job of the Prosecutor easier.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Judges are going to look into the matter. We have two possibilities. The first option is the one suggested by Mr. Stringer; in other words, we are supposed to get the list of documents or the documents gradually, bit by bit, after we resume. The second option is the one proposed by Mr. Kovacic. He'd rather have everything at one go, but he would not mind, so it seems, to getting, at the very least, the list of topics from the Prosecutor. The Judges are going to discuss the matter, and we'll tell you what has been decided. Before I ask you to proceed, Mr. Stringer, I'd like to turn to Mr. Praljak. I listened to you carefully last week as to the notion of defensive action, and I pondered the matter over the weekend. When I have my additional questions, I think it would be useful to hear from you, for you to give useful answers to my questions, I would like to have a map you would prepare yourself, a map in which you're going to position the JNA units before the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina was recognised. I'd like to know where the units were positioned on the ground. I also would like to know the breakdown between the HVO-ABiH forces when the international community recognised the existence of the Republic of BiH. That could be the second card. Another third useful map would be for you to position the HVO and ABiH units in October 1992. I'd like to see where they were positioned respectively. Fourth map, a map showing where the units were in January. You know that famous ultimatum map in January. We'd like to know where the units were positioned respectively. Other map, positioning of HVO and ABiH in April, in the critical period of April to the 9th of May. I'd like to know where everybody was at the time. Thereafter, it would be useful to have a map showing the HVO-ABiH positions on the 30th of June, when the HVO Muslims leave the units. I'd like to know where everybody is at the time. And then when you took up office on the 24th of July, what was the situation like on the ground, where were the units, so the 101, 113 Brigade, where were they exactly positioned. Last map, it concerns the period of October to November. I'd like to know where the various units were positioned. So unfortunately for you, General Praljak, you know that the Appeals Chamber dismissed your application for provisional release, which means that you have to stay here all this time, and you can use this time to prepare the maps so that we can scrutinise them when we resume. I'm asking all of this of you not because you're forced to stay here, but because I think the maps are useful. I have a problem with this concept of defensive action, and I want to make sure that these were defensive actions and not offensives. That's why it's important to see, through the maps, what happened exactly. Are we talking about micro or mega-military operations, and if we can compare the various positionings throughout the dates, we would have a better grasp of the situation. This is not going to happen tomorrow. After the Prosecutor's cross-examination, there will be additional questions and re-examination, and I will have questions about Gornji Vakuf and the maps. Of course, I could work on the documents we have, but you are better placed than I am to tell us where the HVO units were. And, of course, what you're going to prepare will be assessed by the Judges based on the evidence they have already. So this being said, you may proceed, Mr. Stringer.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Mr. President, could I just make one brief reply to Mr. Kovacic's remarks about this issue of disclosure, because it's very important to us. We think what's happening, it's quite clear they want advance disclosure of the topics for cross, they want advance disclosure of the documents that we're going to be using on cross-examination, so the witness can go away, study these things over the break, think about them, think about what his responses are going to be. That's never been the case for any cross-examination in this trial, and in our view it really undermines the essence of cross-examination itself. And so that's why we feel very strongly about this issue, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] To cut a long story short, we are absolutely not asking the Prosecutor to give us the documents in advance. We will be satisfied with a list and a list of topics. As soon as possible, we would like to receive topics and, immediately after the recess, a list of documents under each topic. We are not asking for the Prosecutor to provide us with the documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Bench will discuss this, and will let you know what we've decided.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Mr. Kovacic, it would be helpful to me, at least, but I think perhaps also to my colleagues, if you could explain to us why you attach so much importance to this because, in our experience, once a witness is under cross-examination, his side, so to speak, mainly listens and is prepared to intervene if something goes wrong, which is normally on the spot immediately recognised, so then at one point, of course, there will be the possibility of redirect. We are aware of that. But I do not quite see why this requires the kind of disclosure you are asking for. It's a technical question I'm putting.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, with your leave, I'll answer your question. We're making this request, first and foremost, because this is how we have always proceeded in this courtroom. But it's not just because of that principle, because of common practice, and for the sake of having a fair trial, but it is, above all, for practical reasons that we are making this request. As you are well aware, in this courtroom the translation of a document has frequently been inappropriate, so I'd like to check the documents before they're shown to the witness. When I have the time to have a look at the document in my office, I can see the mistakes, so it's good to go through the documents in details, to go through the translation in details, because initially we might not notice the mistake. It's important to make this objection immediately, as soon as the document is presented, because we all know, on the basis of our experience, that on occasion we have spent a lot of time on dealing with certain issues, on dealing with certain problems, because the documents had translation errors. Furthermore, I would like to make this request when we're dealing with voluminous documents. We need to see whether something has been taken out of context. The last document we consulted on Friday, well, it took us quite a while to see what -- where this extract was from, because we have one heading, one extract from a complete report. No harm was caused, but it's a good example. So to be brief, this is for practical reasons that we're making this request in this courtroom. It's not sufficient for me -- well, two minutes don't suffice to see whether there's a translation error in a document, or if there's a voluminous document, we might see that it hasn't been signed, so the issue of authenticity is then raised, and so on and so forth. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Praljak.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Stringer.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: General, I want to take you back to the 4th of May of this year, which is the date that you began your testimony, and I'm looking now at page 39500 of the transcript, and this relates to the situation in East Mostar during the summer of 1993. This is what you said. You were asking a series of rhetorical questions, if I can put it that way. You said: "How come that the authorities in East Mostar, after the attack of the BH Army on the 9th of May, 1993, and the cease-fire that was agreed after that, did not ask to inspect the main pipes on the boulevard and the main valves there?" Talking about water: "Why didn't they amend the pipes across the Old Bridge. After the attack of the BH Army and the treason of the HVO," I think you mean, well, "treason of the HVO on the part of the Muslim members of the HVO on the 30th of June, 1993, why didn't the authorities in East Mostar engage the UNPROFOR and present to them the problem of water like they did the problem of the wounded and the latter was then resolved?" Do you remember giving that evidence or that statement during your beginning testimony?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do. I spoke about that matter. I believe the quote is correct, although I think that I was speaking about the entire year, since the time that the bridge was destroyed. And I also mentioned this water problem, the fact that it hadn't been fixed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Now, in your binder, if you look at Exhibit P02611, you'll see that that is a document, a letter, dated the 2nd of June, 1993, which is after the day of the conflict on the 9th of May, 1993. And you'll see that this is a letter from Arif Pasalic to UNHCR and also THW, which was the German company that was there to fix the water. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I've got it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Well, and just looking through this document, what he's sending across to them is a proposal for the solution of the water supply problem on the left bank, and you'll see on the second paragraph, this is the second page of the English version, second paragraph of this proposal, he says that: "For the moment being, the complete left bank is supplied by water through four temporary crossings of plastic pipes having diametres of 2 inches and 5/4 inches." And he goes on: "Such quantity of water is not sufficient to comply with the needs of the above-number of inhabitants," et cetera. And then on page 2, at the top, he continues: "From all the above mentioned and in order to avoid catastrophe, the priority task is realisation of temporary and partial rebuilding of water supply system on the left bank." And then at the bottom, at the end, he says: "We are also stressing that inhabitants of the left bank are ready to bear extraordinary efforts and give help to the whole action, including all the structures of civilian protection and the BH Army." So would you agree with me, General, that despite what you said or suggested in your testimony on the 5th -- or the 4th of May, at least here on the 2nd of June we do have an official in East Mostar, Arif Pasalic, who is complaining about the water situation in East Mostar?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Stringer, I wouldn't agree with that. First of all, that wasn't a task for Arif Pasalic. He was a commander in the army, and this was a task for the civilian structures because they dealt with such issues. Secondly, Mr. Stringer, it's quite explicitly stated here that the urban area was no longer being supplied by -- with water after the bridges were destroyed, and that was in 1992, in May and June of 1992. That's when the bridges were destroyed. This letter was drafted one year later. Furthermore, if the left bank was provided for a year in this meagre manner, with two inches and five-fourths of an inch, well, then there is no reason to believe that the civilian structures within the HVO wouldn't have allowed the 250- to 500-millimetre pipes to be made. They didn't do anything about this, although the commission, the joint Croatian and Muslim commission, worked on this, but when they attack, when they were preparing for an offensive, they said that this would be done. Naturally, I don't know what happened, but allow me, if I may, just one more sentence.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: The question is --

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: -- ties back to what you said on the 4th of May, when you suggested that there were no complaints coming from the BH authorities. Will you turn to the next document, P02923. I'm told this one's -- it's a confidential document that can't be shown outside the courtroom, but we can talk about it. This is a report of the ECMM, dated 24 June 1993, and this relates to a meeting in which various individuals were present, and there's a reference to a Mr. Bilic, who is from the armija. And then looking at the third page of the English version, General, it says -- this is the ECMM report. It says: "In the east side, Mr. Bilic has told us again that they have run out of food, water, medicines, et cetera. Some diseases have broken out, stomach, skin, et cetera, due to they have no running water." So would you agree with me, General, that in fact here on the 24th of June, you have another person with the -- among the BH authorities or the BH Army complaining to the internationals about the lack of water in East Mostar?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: There's no doubt that Eastern Mostar had a little less water than Western Mostar. I didn't say that was in dispute. All I am saying is that this was caused by the HVO, because in the previous document it says that a pipe was laid over the Musala Bridge and this organisation should have delivered other constructions -- other equipment, and then the water supply was to be activated, the water was to be disinfected. So you want to solve a very difficult technical problem in three minutes with pipes that were very small in diametre. It's not possible and it's not the HVO's fault. It's the fault of those on the left side, their lack of activity. And it's true that at the time they had already started launching attacks.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Now, the next document in your binder is P03532.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Praljak, in the last document we've seen, there might be a reason that explains the fact that the water is not supplied. Look at paragraph 5, the last paragraph, number 5. It seems that at that time, i.e., when this report was drafted in June, that the German company, THW, returned to Germany. I had -- I was under the impression that they had been assigned to supply East Mostar with water, and now it states that the company has gone back to Germany. How do you interpret this sentence?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, in the previous document they said that the company was late in delivering some complex items, they were 20 days late. It had to do with delivering construction to bridge the river Neretva, and this document was drafted on the 24th of June. On the 24th of June, according to my information, the BH armija had started opening fire on the HVO. We have documents about the losses suffered by the HVO, the number of dead; naturally, the Serbs who were also firing around the bridge. The pipe broke, and people probably returned because they didn't see the possibility of completing their work either because of the war or because for one year the joint commission hadn't worked on the delivering water to the Eastern -- to Eastern Mostar, in particular concerned the northern part that was in the hands of the armija. It had nothing to do with the HVO at all. I'm talking about the source in the direction of Rastani. I have demonstrated this, that Rastani was under the control of the ABiH, and the water at the time had nothing to do with the HVO, apart from the fact that those sources aren't sufficient in summer, when it comes to supplying Mostar with water. It's not sufficient to supply the left bank or the right bank, that if you have a 2 inch pipes and 4/5ths of an inch pipe, well, this just means they didn't care. And then if you blame the HVO for this, well, this is just wrong, it's incorrect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Praljak, irrespective of the fact that everyone was firing at everybody else at the time, I stand to be corrected, this German company, THW, had been called in to get the system to work again. These people were technicians, and everybody agreed that these people should be working there, and then all of a sudden they leave. Since they have left, who could have replaced them to do the same job?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, no one could have replaced them. The pipes that were there, well, they've listed the pipes. The pipes under the bridges were of a diametre between 250 and 500 millimetres. It's the Carinski Bridge and then the Marshal Tito Bridge, 280 millimetres in diametres for the pipes. The Lucki Bridge, 300 millimetre pipes; Hasan Brkic Bridge, 500 millimetres; the Aviation Bridge, 300 millimetres. So this is work for a big company. It involves a lot of money and it would take several months to do. No one in Mostar could carry out this work, even in theory. These bridges were destroyed at the end of May and beginning of June 1992. The telephone exchange and the pipes were destroyed at the time, at the same time, and it says here -- in another document it says that pipes were laid over the Musala Bridge and for other water supply systems there were other pipes, but the construction wasn't delivered, and it says it arrived "20 days ago." So this German company either wasn't interested anymore or it didn't have enough assistance or enough money. Whatever may be the case, the problem that was the result of the Serbian shelling of bridges was a problem that should have be solved in the course of that year, but at that time it's not a problem that could have been solved in Mostar in any way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Stringer.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: General, just a moment ago you said something here. I'm going to read your words back to you. What you said is: "Well, this just mean --" "this just meant, if I could put it that way, "they didn't care, they didn't care." Are you suggesting that the Bosnian authorities of the -- the Bosnia-Herzegovina authorities on the east side were not interested in restoring the water supply, that for some reason they didn't want that to happen?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, Mr. Stringer, I'm not saying that. It's simple. If someone for a year really wanted -- passionately wanted to do something, asked for assistance, and said, We have a problem, summer is going to arrive, well, the problem should have been dealt with. It's a -- well, I'd like to do this, but maybe the Americans or the French should come and do this for us because we have a problem. It's not a matter of not wanting to do this; it's a matter of not wanting to do this sufficiently. A year is sufficient time to do much under such conditions, in my opinion. Well, look, Your Honours --

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Excuse me. I think you've answered the question, which was about whether or not -- [overlapping speakers].

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Now, actually staying with this document, which is P02923, continuing on in the same paragraph 5 about the water, what -- there's a statement here that says that: "There was broken water, too, which is dropping water continuously on the main important part of the base," talking about the Stari Most, the Old Bridge: "When they went to repair it, the HVO fired the workers, and they had to withdraw," suggesting that the workers were fired upon by the HVO when they tried to repair the pipe on the Stari Most. So that's really what happened, General, despite the fact that in your statement of the 4th of May, you suggested that they didn't do anything to try to fix the pipes across the Old Bridge. In fact, they did, and they were fired upon by HVO forces; isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that's not true. The HVO didn't have a position there from which it could have used infantry weapons to open fire on the Old Bridge. You can see that given the positions of the HVO and the ABiH and if you have a look at the factual situation, if you go to the site, because apart from Hum, it's impossible to see the Old Bridge and target it with artillery. Secondly, why would the HVO let soldiers and weapons pass through only to open fire on a pipe that was being repaired so that they would not have water, these being five-fourths-of-an-inch or two-inch pipes? This is just something that the ABiH said. It's just one of the many lies that they spread, that they told to the international observers.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: The next exhibit is P03532. Again, in getting back to your statement on the 4th of May, that here on -- after the 30th of June, why didn't the authorities in East Mostar engage the UNPROFOR and present to them the problem of water, this is an UNPROFOR report dated the 18th of July, 1993, which is after the 30th of June. And this is also a confidential document, Mr. President, and I think it can't be shown outside. And there is a reference here to a civilian authority in the Muslim part of Mostar, Mr. Klaric, I'm looking at the top of page 2. This is item number 2A: "Due to the HVO blockade, 35.000 people in the east bank are without electricity, water supply, and other essential needs. Consequently, a serious threat of epidemic already exists in this part of the city." So here, in fact, despite what you suggested to the Trial Chamber on the 4th of May, General, in fact here we have a civilian authority in East Mostar who is specifically raising the issue of water and the conditions in East Mostar with the UNPROFOR; isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't understand the question about water, about delivering water in a reservoir. How do you understand this issue of water? Is it a glass of water? This water issue, what does it mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Well, let me rephrase the question, then. On the 4th of May, you said, rhetorically: "Why didn't the authorities in East Mostar engage the UNPROFOR and present to them the problem of water?" That's what you said to the Trial Chamber. Now, what I'm doing, General, is I'm showing this document and I'm suggesting to you that, in fact, the authorities did raise the issue of water with UNPROFOR and that when you said otherwise, or suggested otherwise, on the 4th of May, you were wrong. The fact is they did raise the issue of water supply with the UNPROFOR, didn't they?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what it seems like in this document. When I said that they didn't address the issue of water and didn't contact UNPROFOR about this issue or about the issue of the wounded, well, I said on that occasion that the UNPROFOR didn't come to my headquarters and they didn't address the issue of water, as they did address the issue of the wounded. The issue of the wounded was solved. The issue of water couldn't have been solved because it was a technically difficult one, but it could have been dealt with to a certain extent. As I said, electronic motors, generators, could have been used to pump water from Neretva through some pipes, and water could have been delivered, water that was drinkable, it was clean at the time. So that is the answer that I can give you. And there's one other thing --

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Excuse me.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Then after having looked at this document, and we can look at more of them, would you agree with me that you were wrong when you suggested that the authorities in East Mostar did not raise the issue of water with the authorities -- the internationals such as UNPROFOR? You were wrong when you said that on the 4th of May, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I wasn't wrong, because with regard to the issue of -- addressing the issue of water with UNPROFOR, well, I related that to the fact that UNPROFOR didn't tell me about this. They tell me, Here, well, come and fix the water problem while we're attacking. When the HVO responds, someone will die, and then HVO will be the aggressor. So this is a perfidious game that wasn't solved for a year. And then the ABiH says, Come and fix this. They send, for example, a delegation, and then they fire on the HVO, and then they say the HVO has launched an attack. That's how it's presented to the world. So this is very perfidious and it's a problem that wasn't solved for a year. When they attacked --

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: And, Mr. Stringer, look, if they have Bijelo Polje, the north of Mostar, and Rastani, why do they need the HVO to fix the water problem? They don't need the HVO.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: This is the point: You suggested that the BH authorities never complained about the water to the UNPROFOR. That was incorrect, wasn't it? In fact, they did complain to the UNPROFOR.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Praljak, it seems that in this document, the ABiH authorities did mention the problem. Well, the ABiH authorities, let's say the civilian authorities, Mr. Klaric, who at 10.00 in the morning on the 17th of July, 1993, over the radio mentions a series of problems; amongst others, as Mr. Stringer has just told you, the fact there is the problem with the water, and Mr. Klaric says to the UNPROFOR representative in charge of civilian affairs that they have the feeling that the international community has abandoned them. But when you look at the document, you see that at 20 hours on the same day, i.e., 10 hours after, the Civilian Affairs Department of UNPROFOR meet Mr. Stojic, and we have the minutes of the meeting in question. Strangely enough, unless I am mistaken, the problem of the water is not -- does not figure on the minutes of the meeting. This surprises me somewhat. If UNPROFOR realises that the situation as regards water is disastrous, then they should have addressed the matter and discussed it with Mr. Stojic. In that case, Mr. Stojic would have certainly taken stock of the situation. In this case here, Mr. Stojic does not mention water at all. How do you interpret this, General Praljak?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour Judge Antonetti, first of all, a military has nothing whatsoever to do with the problem of water. Let's be clear. And I'm talking about this because I know the situation. At that particular moment, the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina controlled a big source, and a complete territory from that source to the eastern part of Mostar, and I've already said that very loud and clear, and I've even drawn you a map showing where that was, and it is beyond comprehension -- well, they did not need HVO help to bring water to East Mostar. They had the source of Rastani, the territory of Rastani. They had the territory of Bijelo Polje, which is north of Mostar, and the entrance into Mostar, and the Croats the railway bridge. There had been a branch of the water supply. All they had to do was get some pipes and purify the water, and they did not need the HVO at all. But what they want is something completely different. All the time, they were accusing the other side just to cover up their own military operations, and that's the long and the short of it. They never mentioned the water. Everything they wanted, everything they -- we offered them, the hospital, the medicines, the wounded, everything they wanted from us, the HVO offered them, as Mr. Stojic says expressly here, If you so want, we will transfer all the children while the combat is going on, while your offensive is going on. We want to avoid any victims. That's the position of the HVO. The HVO told them, We will transfer the civilians and leave just the soldiers to wage the battle. That was the HVO position all the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Mr. Praljak, I have two questions. One relates immediately to this. I'm surprised that no one told UNPROFOR that the ABiH had sufficient water and the possibility to bring it to East Mostar. I see no trace that anybody, in response to the complaints of the East Mostar authority, came up and said, Look, you have your own water, you can get it, and told UNPROFOR, Why do they complain, they have their own water? I do not understand why no trace of this is found in these documents.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Judge Trechsel, Your Honour, because documents are weak. They don't even say 5 per cent of what was said at the meeting. And everybody picks and chooses whatever suits them best. As far as I was informed, they were told at the meetings very exactly where their sources were, and we saw documents, and a witness was here talking about their control of the source, the territory, the pipes. All they had to do was cross the river, cross the Neretva, and bring water to East Mostar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I have two questions, Mr. Stringer. I'm sorry. I would like to ask the other one too. A while ago, Mr. Praljak, you have said that the HVO had no possibility of firing at the bridge because for a moment it was not possible. When I heard this, it came to my mind that we have seen videos of a tank which, for whatever reasons, was situated on territory which was under the control of the HVO and was firing at the bridge. Now, I seem to detect a certain contradiction there which I would invite you to clarify.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour Judge Trechsel, I said just the opposite. I said that from Hum you could open artillery fire on the Old Bridge. I didn't say that it wasn't possible. I said that it was, indeed, possible, and that from Hum you could destroy the Old Bridge in a minute at any point in time. And I also said that fire was not opened from Hum on the Old Bridge even when the military were crossing, when the arms were being transported across the bridge, when the repairmen were repairing the pipeline. I said that you could not see the Old Bridge with infantry weapons from the HVO positions in Mostar. I don’t know how it was interpreted, but I expressly said that one could open artillery fire from Hum and target the Old Bridge. And I already said earlier that if I had wanted to destroy the bridge I would have done that in the matter of minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Praljak. In fact, it says "apart from Hum." I wonder perhaps the "apart" was not in the transcript when I saw it, but you are right in that point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General, in relation to what you have just said, we saw a video showing the tank firing at the bridge, but my memory is very good, and I remember that there were tracer bullets. How do you account for that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't understand the word "tracer." What do you mean, when it hits or -- when you're recording a tank shell with a camera, you can actually see it, you can see its trajectory, but it all depends on the casing, whether it will explode immediately or with a delay. Different casings can be used for different types of artillery tools.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Praljak, your counsel, over the recess, may have a look at this video again. He will see that when the tank fires at the bridge, at the same time you can see tracer bullets straight -- with a straight trajectory and hitting the bridge. Where was the one who fired the tracer bullets? Where could he be, if not on the Hum hill?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour, Hum is up there, and judging by the trajectory of the projectiles, I was with some people, some of those shells were not from a tank, and my impression was that fire was not open only by that assumed tank that you can't see very well, but that there was a third party which was not the HVO that opened fire on the bridge at the time using an artillery weapon that wasn't a tank. Looking at the trajectory in the direction of Neretva - but let me just finish - and from the north side something hit the bridge, there is a rubber [as interpreted] and there is a flash of light. I tried to talk to experts to ask them where the projectile came from. I even raised the issue in a television show, stating that a shell came from the BiH Army side and that its calibre was smaller than a tank calibre. But it did not come from Hum, and you can tell that very clearly from its trajectory.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, so you are saying that the tracer bullets that can be seen were fired not from where the tank was positioned, but from an area under ABiH control, and you say that it was the ABiH that fired the bullets, not the HVO; is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] With a high degree of certainty. I raised the issue publicly, I can't claim that for a fact, but I believe that with a very high degree of certainty.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Those who have time on their hands can do what I'm going to do, view the video, and they will see very clearly tracer bullets hitting the bridge.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Tracer bullets of some kind, yes. I said that publicly on a TV show. I asked that, I showed that. I asked for answers. Nobody came forth, and the question that I raised was: Where did this come from? It came from the northern side. There was a huge ball, there was a shadow of the explosion, that's what we saw.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: General, the next exhibit is P03925. 3925. If you would find that one in your binder, please. This is also under seal. General, just getting back to this -- the main point here, which is whether BH authorities complained to UNPROFOR about the water situation in East Mostar, this is a report of the Spanish Battalion, dated 3 August 1993, and this is item number 1.2, page 4 of the English. And 1.2, subparagraph 1, says -- this is in the Spanish Battalion report: "According to BH -- Bosnia-Herzegovina sources in the town, the first cases of typhoid have been recorded in the Muslim part of the town, as a consequence of drinking untreated water directly from the River Neretva." And so again, General, here is another reference in the UNPROFOR documents about appeals and complaints about the water situation in Mostar being made to the UNPROFOR; isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't find it. Could you please direct me to the page number?

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: This is a -- if you look, you'll see section 1 is "Zone of Influence," and then there is 1.1, which is the routes. Do you see that, 1.1, which is about the routes, the roads?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. Well, nothing --

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And then if you continue, you'll get to 1.2, which is about areas, and underneath that there is a reference to Mostar and shelling. And then underneath that, it says "Other Reports," and then paragraph 1: "According to the BiH sources in the town, the first cases of typhoid have been recorded as a consequence of drinking untreated water directly from the River Neretva." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: So, again, despite what you said on the 4th of May, in fact, the BH authorities in East Mostar were reporting the situation to the UNPROFOR throughout this period of time which falls after the 30th of June. Would you agree with me that this issue was reported to the UNPROFOR on a repeated basis?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Here UNPROFOR conveys what the Bosnian-Herzegovinian sources in town report, that's all. This is not a confirmation on the part of UNPROFOR. It just says, The Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina told us this and that. I don't really don't think much of this, and if you want me to, I'll show you all other --

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: I'm not asking you what you think of this. I'm asking you about your prior sworn testimony here, when you claimed that they did not engage the UNPROFOR and present to them the problem of water. I'm reading to you from what you said under oath on the 4th of May. The fact is that's not true, is it? They did present to UNPROFOR the water problem, didn't they? Would you agree with me that you were wrong on the 4th of May when you said that?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. You always want to leave out one part of my testimony and you want to turn me into somebody with a very low IQ and purport that I should know what they told UNPROFOR. What I said was that they did not provide UNPROFOR with any information they [as interpreted] reached me. I'm not such a stupid man to say that I know what you said to your associate. What I said was that the UNPROFOR never raised the problem with the HVO, as they raised the issue of the wounded which was then resolved. Please, don't make me look stupid. Don't underestimate my intelligence. I'm not lying here.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Maybe we will save time. I believe that there has been a misunderstanding in dates. Maybe I have a -- I did not hear my colleague well. The report was drafted on the 3rd of August, 1993, so this was after the 30th of June, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Well, let me just read again from the general's testimony on the 4th of May. This is what he said: "After the attack of the BH Army and the treason of the HVO, on the part of the Muslim members of the HVO, on the 30th of June, 1993, why didn't the authorities in East Mostar engage the UNPROFOR and present to them the problem of water?" That's what he said. Now, here we're talking about specifically the time-frame after the 30th of June.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: So let's see perhaps, General, if we can put it to you this way: When you said that they didn't present the issue of water to the UNPROFOR, would you agree with me that that's not correct? In fact, they did present the issue of water to the UNPROFOR after the 30th of June?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I do not agree with that, either, because my sentence says precisely this. I am a logician and please don't make me -- no, no. My sentence, if it has been translated properly from Croatian, it says they did not present the problem to UNPROFOR that UNPROFOR would then implicitly complain to me. Sir, there's no chance for you to receive from me something based on an incomplete sentence or implying what I said. It will not happen. I don't lie, I am not an imbecile, I will never collide my own sentences. That's why --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Praljak, do you agree that the UNPROFOR was informed, prior to the 3rd of August, that, from what they said - maybe they lied, but we don't know that - they said that there were cases of typhoid that were the consequences of people getting water from the River Neretva and drinking untreated water, that that was the cause for typhoid cases? Do you agree that that is what is said in this document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If UNPROFOR had told us, We were in hospital, our doctor was there, we stated there was a case of typhoid, I would have believed that. This is just war propaganda which was spinned by a lying team called the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina. This is propaganda, that's what I'm aware. If there were cases of typhoid, then there were medical records on those cases, so the Prosecutor should provide us with the written record of the cases of typhoid in East Mostar.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: General, before we move to the next document, let me ask you this. We're going to come back to this later when we talk more about East Mostar. Based on what you've said, at least today, your position is that the ABiH, the armija, did have the ability to restore the water service to East Mostar if they wanted to do it, that they just didn't do that for whatever reason; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The BiH Army, I repeat, had control, after the 30th of June, over a large source of water, one of the two main sources of water for the city of Mostar. It had continuous control over the territory from that place and a water-pipe to the Neretva River. All they had to do was to bridge the Neretva River. They received a huge amount of money from the international institutions of Muslim countries, and whether they decided to spend that money on those things or not, it's not up to me to speculate what they did. As far as I know, they had enough money, and I absolutely know that they had their own source, they had the means to bring water to wherever they wanted to. Why they didn't do that, it's not up to me to speculate.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Do you deny that, in fact, the water situation in East Mostar, and the humanitarian situation in general in East Mostar after the 30th of June, 1993, do you deny that the situation there was, in fact, disastrous for the population in East Mostar? Do you agree with that or no?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I deny that completely. It wasn't disastrous. Look at any of the footage recorded by the international monitors. You will see that the situation of those people is anything but disastrous. They never had a shortage of food. All that is propaganda. You should -- you would be best advised to look at the tapes and see what people looked like, the same people who pretended that their situation was disastrous.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Well, let's look at some tape, then. Mr. President, we have a small segment from a video that's in evidence, P06365. It's in Sanction, and it's just very short, just a few seconds. We'll show that, and then I'll ask the general some questions about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: "The man on the right died, but managed to save the other man. Not long afterwards, another emergency. A woman was lying on the riverbank. She had been doing her family's washing. She was already dead, shot by a Croat sniper."

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Could we be advised what is the date of this shooting?

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: It's P0365 and it's in evidence. It's the Bowen BBC documentary called "Unfinished Business." It's from August and September of 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Now, General --

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can we please go --

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Let me ask you a question. If you want to see it again, we can come back to it, I assure you, we'll show it again. What I want to do first, though, is take you to the next document, which is P04440, 4440. This is another document that I think is confidential, Mr. President, an ECMM report. Do you have that document, General?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Could you repeat the number of that document? I've not got it, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: 4440, ECMM report dated 23 August 1993. 4440.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: 4440, yes, okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: It's an ECMM report.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: And what is the question about the document that you showed me previously? I don't know what is the direction of the flow of the Neretva, whether the woman was wounded on the left or the right bank. I believe that it was on the right bank, which excludes that it was done by the HVO. But I believe that you should approach all such matters with all due respect towards the dead people, you know.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Paragraph 2 of this document, General, in front of you relates to a meeting with the UNHCR, and the ECMM report is reporting that according to him, HVO snipers kept the population even --

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not receiving a translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: I'll start again. It's all right. Can you hear me now?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: [In English] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: All right. Paragraph 2 of this report, concerning the situation in Mostar, reporting about HVO snipers kept the population even from getting water from the Neretva River, urging the international organisations put severe pressure on getting access to the east bank for humanitarian aid convoys as soon as possible. So with this document and the video footage that we've just seen, General, would you agree with me that, in fact, the water situation in East Mostar was so bad that people were forced to risk their life by trying to get down to the river to get water to drink and to do laundry?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Interpretation] From the tape you showed us, I can't conclude a thing. I can only conclude that a person was killed, a man was killed. And the woman lying on the bank, I believe that she's lying on the right bank, given the direction of the flow, and this excludes any possibility, if you know what the banks of the Neretva look like, that they are very steep, and the Judges saw that for themselves. In 95 per cent of the places in Mostar, you can descend down to the river and not be visible from anywhere but from the first row of houses close to the river. I now repeat, I exclude any possibility that an HVO sniper, save for in some places, but in 95 per cent of the places if you come to get water from the Neretva, you can't be targeted except from the positions of the BiH Army. And as for humanitarian convoys at --

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: I'm asking you about the water. We're trying to limit this to the water in your statement at the beginning of your testimony, General. So we've got your answer, and I'm going to move on to the next topic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Praljak, you know Mostar. The Judges know Mostar a little because we went there, but we did not know the situation back in 1993. Is it a tradition in Mostar for women to go and do their laundry in the Neretva River? Is that something customary or, as is suggested by the Prosecutor, is it so that this lady could not do her washing at home and, as could be seen in the footage, she went to the bank to do her laundry? Because we can see her laundry on a rock, so she had to dip her laundry in -- she was putting the laundry into the river when she was hit. These are terrible pictures, of course, because you can see her lying dead, hit by a bullet, on the ground. I'd like to know this: Did it happen that women would go and do their laundry in the river, as is done in many countries in the world, or is this a case when she went to the river because she had no water at home?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can't answer that question with regard to that woman, but I know that in Mostar, before I went to university, I always did the laundry for my mother by going down to the Neretva River. We would go down to the river to do the laundry, in particular when we had to wash sheets, such items. Later, I don't know how frequently this was done, but all civilians who were killed, and we've seen hundreds -- thousands of civilians who were killed, and it's terrible when we see such images, unfortunately this continues ad infinitum. But what is interesting here is -- well, I'm not sure, but if we could have a look at it again, I think she's on the right bank. Your Honours, if you can remember what the Neretva looks like, the banks were like this [indicates]. Someone at the bottom of the Neretva, well, could be hit in this way. It's from an angle of 45 degrees from above. So it's not possible -- 90 [as interpreted] per cent of the places you can go down to the Neretva, it's not possible to hit someone in such places unless you're firing from a building by the Neretva or from the bank of the Neretva. You can check this and you can say, Praljak, you're just a liar, Mostar is still there, the Neretva River is still there, and the houses are still there. I went swimming in the Neretva, I went down there in Santiceva Street where I lived, and I was very familiar with the situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: I think it's time for the break, Mr. President. I don't know if you want to break at this point or --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, you're quite right. I had completely forgotten about our break. We shall have a 20-minute break now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Stringer, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: General, I'm going to move on to the next item on this current grouping of documents. Let me ask you if you remember your testimony of the 13th of May this year, during your direct examination, and you were asked this actually by Judge Antonetti, Judge Antonetti asked you - and this is page 40014 of the transcript - Judge Antonetti asked you whether at the time that you were the commander of the HVO Main Staff, which is the time between the 24th of July and the 8th of November, 1993, whether during that time, as Judge Antonetti said: "Since you were in charge of the military operations as commander of the HVO, I'd like to know whether, as far as you know at that time, you felt that, as far as your command was concerned, or maybe as far as the instructions you were obtaining from Mr. Boban ...," and I'm skipping down, "Did you feel at the time that the Republic of Croatia actually played a role in the military operations that you led?" And your answer, General, was as follows: "Never, Your Honour, not even Boban told me anything at any point ...," and now the part I'm interested in: "At the time that I was commander, I think that I met with Mr. Boban only briefly on two occasions." I'm skipping down a couple of lines. You say: "During that time I never saw, I never spoke, I never met with Mr. Franjo Tudjman, and I think that I saw Gojko Susak only on one occasion, I think." And then skipping down, you said: "I saw Gojko on that occasion because he had been visiting with his mother, who lived near Siroki Brijeg. We met very briefly. I told him that we managed to restore the lines, and he never influenced in any way, never said anything ..." So skipping down, this is line 23, page 40015, you said it again: "I never spoken to Franjo Tudjman, and I think that I only met and spoke with Gojko Susak on that day when he came to visit his mother." Now, General, the next exhibit in the binder there is one of the presidential transcripts, and this is P05080, and it is a meeting with President Tudjman, Mate Boban, and others, including yourself, on the 15th of September, 1993. So let me ask you first, General, on the 15th of September, 1993, were you, in fact, the commander of the HVO Main Staff?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And do you -- I can direct you to page 18 of the transcript, and you can see that your name appears there. Actually, I'm sorry, page -- that's right, page 18. President Tudjman invites you to speak. Do you see that? Page 18.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And as is indicated on the top of page 1, Mate Boban was also present at this meeting. And then if you look at page 18, you'll see also that Gojko Susak -- I'm sorry, not page 18. Page 16, you'll see that Gojko Susak is president and speaks as well. You'll see the reference there to Mate Boban. So, in fact, General, when you testified under oath on the 13th of May that you didn't see, speak to, or meet with Franjo Tudjman during the time that you were commanding the HVO Main Staff, that wasn't true, was it, that wasn't correct? You, in fact, met with him at least on this occasion on the 15th of September in his office?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: The next item, General, relates to your testimony on the 19th of May, and you were asked about -- or you were talking about the meeting that occurred between President Tudjman and President Milosevic in April of 1992 at Karadjordjevo, and on page 2 -- I'm sorry, page 40328 of the transcript, you testified that: "The story --" and I'm reading back your words to you on your direct: "The story about the division of Bosnia-Herzegovina appeared only in 1993." Continuing on, talking about Karadjordjevo: "I claim based on everything I know, on the facts that I'm aware of, that the meeting was not secret, and there is no single participant that will assert it dealt with the division of Bosnia-Herzegovina. That political lie appeared only in 1993 in order to put pressure on Croatia, and only for that reason." And then page 40332 of your testimony, you say: "That story, and this is my experience which I am testifying to, appeared only in 1993, two years subsequently, two years after the meeting, and I know that the story turned up out of the blue because of the political show-downs -- because the political show-downs had started." Do you remember that testimony, General, that you said that stories about the division of Bosnia-Herzegovina coming out of Karadjordjevo only emerged in 1993?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember that, and I said that that was the case according to all of the information I had. At all the meetings I attended, this was never discussed up until 1993, this subject was never discussed up until 1993, or, rather, this story was never told up until 1993. That's when they started spreading the story.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: All right. Now -- and I see that you've turned to what I think is the next exhibit there in your binder, P10968. Do you have that, General, P10968?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One moment. General, before we move on to the next exhibit, what is a real problem is that the Prosecutor is going in one direction and the documents we're seeing are very important documents. It's sometimes difficult to follow the Prosecutor all the way, because we don't know whether the Prosecutor is going to get back to this document at a later stage. I'm caught between a rock and a hard place, because I would like the Prosecutor to develop his case; on the other hand, I am also concerned with establishing the truth. As far as the document we have just seen is concerned, clearly, in light of what Tudjman says and in light of what you say, you didn't always agree with Tudjman. He's asking you for your opinion, and you answer, and according to your answer it seems that there's a slight discrepancy between you two. This is quite clear on page 19, where President Tudjman says this, and this is important because this relates to the joint criminal enterprise, when it took place, when it started, when it ended, because Tudjman here says -- and you are between yourselves, there are no representatives from the international community, there is nobody else, there is Tudjman, Boban, and you yourself and other people, but this is a select committee. And he says this: "But the struggle against the Muslims should stop." His position is clear. There should be no further operations against the Muslims. And you then take the floor again. Do you remember that on that day, this is in the month of September, the 15th of September, to be precise, Tudjman says, in a select committee, to Boban and to you, "The fight against the Muslims should end"? Do you remember this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I can confirm that I attended the meeting and that I did say what is claimed. I forgot about the meeting when giving my testimony, but I stand by what I have said. I don't think there is a discrepancy, although I didn't always agree with Susak or with Boban or with Franjo Tudjman, for the simple reason that I have my own opinions based on facts, and they should be presented quite clearly at each and every meeting, and that is what I did here. But the fighting would end, Your Honour, when the Muslims stopped attacking. I'll repeat this again. I didn't sign for any offensive operations, apart from taking back a hill that had been lost and Rastani that we had lost, so you have to read through the entire text. This agreement was signed. The whole situation is explained, and I spoke about the situation we were in. It's quite clear. Franjo Tudjman's sentence is in the conditional. The fighting against the Muslims should come to an end, should. So this expresses a desire. And I say the fighting will come to an end when -- well, it's quite -- clearly the offensive is petering out. I said Zepce, Kiseljak, Vitez, et cetera, are being supplied, I said how they were being supplied. I stand by this statement. I also said the Muslims wanted to reach Neum. Everything I have repeated is a fact, and what you have here is also a fact.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There's a person whom I don't know. Ivan Milas, who is this person?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ivan Milas is a lawyer by profession. He was living in Austria for a long time. That's where he worked. He had emigrated there. He had a certain position in the HDZ. I don't really know what kind of a position, but he was a high-ranking HDZ official, and he was the guard of the seals in Croatia. That was a somewhat strange position, but that was the title of the position. At the time, he was a member of the parliament.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Stringer, I'm sorry to have interrupted you. I wanted to clarify Tudjman's position on the fighting.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Yeah, Mr. President, thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Tudjman said earlier on that in that agreement, when the international public was addressed, it was necessary to say that the Muslims were attacking us, it was necessary to say how many people had been expelled, and so on and so forth. And I can show you where this is said.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay, General, now I've moved on to the next topic which related to your testimony about Karadjordjevo and your assertion that reporting about an alleged plan to divide Bosnia-Herzegovina didn't emerge until some two years after the meeting. I then directed you to P10968, which is an article written by a gentleman named Muhamed Filipovic. Do you see the article there, do you have it?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And just to remind the Trial Chamber, General, this is the same Muhamed Filipovic whose book you presented to the Trial Chamber during a part of your direct examination; do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: That's Exhibit 3D03554. And on the 18th of May, 2009, actually, what you told the Trial Chamber was that Mr. Filipovic was a participant in the parties in the war. He was a partisan from the year 1943. You went on to talk about his experience and his background as a student of philosophy. He obtained his PhD, was a faculty member at the School of Philosophy in Sarajevo. He authored 10 or 11 books. He was a member of the academia of Bosnia-Herzegovina, one of the most prominent intellectuals, and - these are your words - on the 18th of May: "He's one of the most prominent intellectuals among the ranks of the Muslim Bosniak people in Bosnia-Herzegovina." Now -- so that's Muhamed Filipovic. I'm looking at the first paragraph of this article that he published on the 10th of June, 1991, which is probably only about six weeks or so after the meeting in Karadjordjevo, where he says: "In recent times, reports have been arriving from many sources and from various parties to the effect that an agreement to partition Bosnia-Herzegovina is being prepared between Serbia and Croatia. The first reports on this began to circulate after the meeting, shrouded in secrecy, between Tudjman and Milosevic, first in Karadjordjevo, and then in the vicinity of Osijek. At the time, it was said that while considering aspects of the conflict between Serbia and Croatia, they talked about a partition of Bosnia-Herzegovina similar to what was done through the 1938-1939 Cvetkovic-Macek agreement as a way to resolve the Serbo-Croatian conflict." Now, I'll just continue down in this article from Professor Filipovic. I'm on the second page now, halfway down the second page of the English translation: "Two days ago, Tudjman let it be known at a press conference, although in a rather roundabout way, that work is actually being done on a partition of Bosnia-Herzegovina, but he shifted the burden of this idea, as well its motive, onto Milosevic's policy and Serbian policy in general." And then he continues on with the quote there that we can all read. And then I'm skipping down a paragraph, and what Filipovic says is this: "All of this has been done without us, against us, and against the interests of the majority of the population of Bosnia-Herzegovina, like proprietors of our fate and our country. Naturally, this disregards our own desires, and we Bosnians and Herzegovinians, who have not succumbed to the virus of partition and the corrosion of our body and minds, will bitterly resist this. There are no methods whatsoever for achieving this without violence, but this must be avoided because otherwise it will be responded to in kind." Now, General, the first question is this: When you gave your testimony on the 19th of May, when you claimed that there were no reports about the partition of Bosnia-Herzegovina until 1993, that wasn't correct, was it; that wasn't true? In fact, this very respected man, who you've introduced the Trial Chamber to during your direct examination, this well-respected individual, in fact, reported on this issue of partition coming out of Karadjordjevo, and he did so a mere six weeks after the Karadjordjevo meeting took place; isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: If the date is correct, well, what it says there is then true, but I didn't say that Muhamed Filipovic wrote something said in "Vjesnik," I spoke about the information I had about whether this was something that was being discussed at the time. I said that quite precisely. I said according to the information I had, the issue appeared when pressure was exerted on Croatia in 1993. As far as this text is concerned, I can analyse it item by item, I read through it. Quite clearly, it's just hearsay, speculation. And the second thing is that at the time nothing was done in secret. I've demonstrated this. At none of the meetings of all the presidents of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina was anything done in secret. It was all done with agreement of the international community. Everything was published, everything was in the open, but it was a matter of a proposal made by Alija Izetbegovic and Kiro Gligorov, the president of Macedonia. Very well, very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
