utterances.text: I'll take you back again to what you said under oath on the 19th of May. You said: "The story about the division of Bosnia-Herzegovina appeared only in 1993." I'll keep reading from your testimony, General. You continued and you said, and this is page 40328 of the transcript, you said: "You saw yesterday, Your Honours, that at the same time when this notorious meeting was taking place, Filipovic was talking to Tudjman and Tudjman was offering things for Bosnia and Herzegovina which were totally different, and this was simultaneous." So now, General, based on what you told us in direct, Filipovic is, in fact, having direct communications about Tudjman -- with Tudjman about this issue, and so would you agree with me that he was, in fact, in a much better position than you to give an opinion as to whether the division of Bosnia-Herzegovina was on the table at Karadjordjevo?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course, he wasn't. He went to a meeting with Franjo Tudjman and he spoke about this in his book. He spoke about what was offered to him. He was in the opposition. He was opposed to the political -- he was in opposition with Alija Izetbegovic's programme, and surely at the time in VONS, in the council, I had better information about what was discussed at the meeting, better information than what Muhamed Filipovic had. What he has put down in the text is speculation. Where there is smoke, there is fire, rumours are spread, and things of that nature that are said. He's a prominent intellectual in Bosnia-Herzegovina, but I don't find him that prominent, although I do respect him in certain fields.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Would you then at least agree with me, General, that when you said that the story about the division of Bosnia-Herzegovina appeared only in 1993, would you agree with me, sir, that when you said that, that was wrong? In fact, the story appeared very swiftly after the Karadjordjevo meeting occurred in 1991?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm telling you what I was aware of. I'm telling you about the story that circulated at meetings. I'm telling you about what I heard from people with whom I had contact in Croatia at the time. This is a text by Filipovic that appeared in "Vjesnik" and it's of no relevance with regard to the matter. We are discussing -- the text is correct, but the real story appeared in 1993, once pressure had been exerted on Croatia so that Croatia would give in. And I stand by my testimony, and I don't agree with your interpretation, not at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Let me take you to the last passage that I read from this Filipovic article, where he says that, talking about partition: "There are no methods whatsoever for achieving this without violence." General, would you agree with me that those words were, in fact, quite prophetic, in that anyone who considered partition of Bosnia-Herzegovina, anyone who considered the creation of ethnically-based territories, was, in fact, aware of the strong likelihood that violence would be a result of such a plan?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't understand your question. What does it have to do with? It's a speculative question. I could address this issue for an hour, if you're interested in that. But to provide you an answer to a very complex question very briefly, in a few words, well, I'll refuse to do that. I will not confirm any of your speculations. Filipovic was involved in the historical agreement of Alija Izetbegovic with the Croats -- not the Croats [as interpreted]. Izetbegovic deceived him in the historical agreement. Well, look, if you want the truth, then ask me about the truth. If you want to play games with me so that you can obtain an answer that is not truthful, well, I'll just tell you that I can't answer your question, a question which --

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Now, General --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Prlic has noticed something.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for Mr. Prlic, please. THE ACCUSED PRLIC: I think there is mistake in transcript, because General Praljak mentioned historic agreement among Muslim and Serbs, but in transcript it's mentioned that this is historic agreement of Alija Izetbegovic with Croats. And I take this opportunity to specify that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Praljak, when you talk about a historic agreement, was this between the Muslims and the Serbs or was it between Izetbegovic and the Croats?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Between Izetbegovic and Milosevic and Karadzic and Silajdzic and Mladic at the time. It was a historical agreement that they were reaching according to which Bosnia and Herzegovina was to be taken into Yugoslavia. The Croats had nothing to do with it. They were fully informed about this. Filipovic was involved in this, but Izetbegovic deceived him. Zulfikarpasic worked on this together with Filipovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Praljak, I wonder whether you understood Mr. Stringer's question. When Mr. Stringer showed you the document, he was asking you to confirm or deny Mr. Filipovic's view, who says in this document that if partition -- ethnic partition is to be made, this would result in violence. So Filipovic was ringing the alarm bells at the time. If there was a project aimed at partition, this would mean resorting to violence and war. I think that this is what Mr. Stringer wanted to highlight when he put his question to you, and I don't believe that you understood the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I completely understood the question. First of all, this does not have to be the truth. There were examples where such things happened without any war. The natural division between the Czechs and the Slovaks did not result in a war. The national divisions within the Soviet Union did not result in any conflicts along the ethnic lines. So this does not have to necessarily be the truth. And I have a lot more examples to that effect. Second of all, when it comes to Bosnia and Herzegovina, the international community and Croats never spoke about a national divide, but rather about a dominant national and cultural divide, and the first such divide was proposed by Cutileiro. Why don't you bring Cutileiro and the international community here? They were the first one that proposed that. And this was one of the conditions, if not the condition, of the future referendum. And the first request for the separation or division within the political thought came from the Serb side. They were the ones who occupied the whole story, and then the things went further on as they did, and the Croats participated in that only as a party that was under constant attack by the Serbs and then by the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: I waited for the translation. So, Mr. Praljak, my first question is -- or, rather, remark is that, of course, you make talk about plans like Cutileiro, et cetera, but don't -- I believe it would not be right approach on your behalf if you would then say that all the international efforts aimed at ethnic divisions. I believe that it cannot be held, this position. Definitely, some of the plans like also the Vance-Owen, et cetera, took into account the ethnic and national, in a way, divisions of certain parts of Bosnia-Herzegovina, but always with the approach that the integrity and unity of Bosnia-Herzegovina should be upheld. So I would like to say this, it is what the international plans and proposals represented, and it is another question what has -- what was actual the situation and that those plans did not succeed. And I meant always that please try to slow down and to talk in -- also, frankly sometimes Mr. Stringer is speaking a bit too quickly, but also on your behalf, you should make further efforts, Mr. Praljak, to slow down. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour Judge Prandler, I don't know how this was interpreted. I said expressly that the international plans were not based only or exclusively or -- on international divide, their efforts to keep the dominant population, taking into account cultural, economic, and transport ties, this is what your objection went to, I said they did not, and only Vance-Owen later took into account only partly that certain citizens lived in a certain area as a majority or a -- in any case, the borders of Bosnia and Herzegovina were never questionable, especially not within the framework of the Croatian policy. The Croatian policy never challenged the borders of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, let me address you. I know it is not appropriate to object to a question that has already been asked and answered, but if you allow me, I would, with some delay, like to object to my learned friend Stringer's question which has been recorded on line [as interpreted] 50 of the record, lines from 12 to 16. In my learned friend Stringer's questions, there are two questions. The first part of the question refers to the division of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and the second part of the question refers to the creation of ethnically-based territories, and I assume that this refers to the existing borders of Bosnia-Herzegovina. This means that the question contains two theses to which one can provide two different answers, and I believe that General Praljak's answer and the intervention on the part of His Honour Judge Prandler is the consequence of the fact that the question put by my learned friend Stringer contains two theses that beg for two different answers. Can we just make a distinction and say that we're talking about two different questions that have to be answered and approached in two different ways? I apologise for having intervened.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Stringer, were there two aspects to your question or not?

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Well, Mr. President, I think that we could -- to some extent, we're all interpreting what was written by Mr. Filipovic here, when he's talking about the virus of partition. I can only tell you that as I see it, I don't distinguish between partition within the borders of Bosnia-Herzegovina or whether, in fact, partition is going to involve some changing of the borders of Bosnia-Herzegovina. So I see it -- and the intent of the question was really without distinction as to those two, that when you are talking about creating territories based on ethnicity, violence is quite likely going to result, particularly when some of that territory or all of it falls within the boundaries of a place like Bosnia-Herzegovina. We're going to come back to this, Mr. President, obviously at length as part of the JCE part, and so I was -- I'm satisfied with the answer given by the witness at this stage, and I'm prepared to move on, if that's -- but I see -- I think Judge Trechsel had --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Yes, you see quite correctly, Mr. Stringer. Mr. Praljak, on the same page of this document, there is a passage I would like you to comment upon. It is the third paragraph on page -- the second page, where I read: "Today, we know from reliable sources of the international political public that Tudjman, during his visit to Great Britain, spoke on three occasions about the partition of Bosnia as a real possibility and solution that is acceptable in terms of his policy." Now, you can say that you think that this is not true, or that it -- that Tudjman meant something else, or you can say that you do not want to comment. It's all up to you, but I wanted to give you an opportunity to state your view on this.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My position is as follows: A, Muhamed Filipovic, who does not have any information about the diplomacy of the state that he belongs to, cannot speculate about these things. These are just staple phrases, information from well-informed circles, international circles. You can hear such phrases every day. Whenever somebody wants to raise an issue in newspapers, then this is how they start, We learned from well-informed sources, and then you write whatever after that, you wait for a reaction, and then you -- this is just like launching things. And that's all the comment I have.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to express concern about the arguments provided by my learned friend Stringer which we find on page 55, at the beginning there. I'm afraid that what is implied here is a change in the indictment, because my learned friend says, and I paraphrase, that he does not make a distinction between the division of Bosnia within its boundaries, which means that the changes would involve changes to the boundaries of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and further on he says, when we are talking about the creation of territories based on ethnicities, force will probably have to be used as a result of that, and especially given the fact that some of the territories are within certain boundaries in Bosnia and Herzegovina. This is a new thesis on the part of the Prosecutor. We don't find it in the indictment. If I may paraphrase the indictment, I'm not going to go into legal details of the indictment, the indictment says that Croats and Croats in Bosnia-Herzegovina, through joint criminal enterprise, wanted to take one part of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and what is implied here is that Croats in Bosnia-Herzegovina who were working on special territorial determination to see what ethnicity will have a majority, in what part. In agreement with the international community, starting with Cutileiro, it seems now that this too is the object of incrimination. I know that my learned friend doesn’t think that, but if he would kindly state for the record that he stands by the indictment as written so that we don’t have to wonder at a later stage what the Prosecutor meant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Wait a minute, General Praljak. Mr. Stringer has to answer, since your lawyer raised a legal point as to the scope of the indictment, asking whether there was any change to the Prosecution's case, so we've got to give Mr. Stringer an opportunity to be more specific.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Well, Mr. President, again this is cross-examination. I'm not purporting to make speeches about the scope of the indictment. It says what it says, and I can assure the Trial Chamber that the Prosecution's theory on the scope of the JCE is not changed. So that's -- that's that. It's not changed in the least. Now, again, I -- we're going to come back to this whole JCE issue, and my strong preference, if I can put it that way, Mr. President, is if I could just continue with this part of the cross. We're going to be in a position to discuss these issues in detail at some length at a later time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: General Praljak, setting aside the Filipovic article now, I want to -- we have mentioned --

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: But --

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: We have mentioned Karadjordjevo, and it's time for us to move on to talk a little bit more about that. And at one point during your direct examination on the 19th of May, you talked about the testimony that President Stipe Mesic gave in this Tribunal in Karadjordjevo, and I'm looking at page 40330 of the transcript on the 19th of May, in which you said that: "Stipe Mesic perjured himself and he was telling lies here, and he did that because he wanted to retaliate against Franjo Tudjman. Mr. Mesic did not present truthful facts." Do you remember that testimony, General?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you are quoting accurately, then yes, I did state that. I would kindly ask you, when you are quoting from my statement, then quote, don't paraphrase. There is a quote, state the page, the line, and then say, I quote, so that I don’t have to comment upon your interpretation by saying "yes" or "no". Give me a quote and I’ll say, yes, that’s right. I’m not going to confirm your interpretation of my words. Please.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: I'm not interpreting. I'm reading from the transcript. But I -- because you're taking the interpretation, I'll try to be more clear about when I'm reading your words. But I can assure you, General, that I'm just reading your words as they appear on the transcript, and the transcript says that according to you, you said, and I'm quoting: "Stipe Mesic perjured himself and he was telling lies here ..." So, General, do you recall that testimony?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I remembered this, and I adhere by my words.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Now, I want to talk a little more about that, in Karadjordjevo, which the meeting itself, I believe I'm correct in saying, it occurred at the end of March of 1991; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: This happened on the date when it happened. You have to say the exact date, not "towards the end of March or thereabouts." If you have the date, please state the date. And you do have the date.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: At the end of March 1991, General, you were not a member of the Croatian Army, were you?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Nor were you a member of the Government of the Republic of Croatia; correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: These meetings, if there were meetings taking place between President Tudjman and other members of his cabinet or his government, you were not participating in those meetings at that time, were you?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct, I wasn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Now, I believe, and correct me if I'm wrong because I don't have the transcript reference for this, I believe that something you said in your earlier direct testimony indicated to us that during the spring of 1991, you were in the Sandzak region, shooting some documentaries, filming some documentaries. Is that what you were doing at the time Karadjordjevo took place?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I can't confirm that I -- while the meeting in Karadjordjevo was taking place, that I was in Sandzak at that precise time. I was there for a very short period of time, in Sandzak, shooting a documentary, but I was following newspapers very closely. I was informed about the meetings of all presidents of all the republics. Rest assured that my journey to Sandzak was not only aimed at shooting the documentary, but also to investigate the situation in Sandzak, because big Serb rallies had taken place there. On the eve of my arrival there, Vuk Draskovic held a huge rally. About 100.000 people turned up.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Now, on the other hand, would you agree with me that President Mesic was, in fact, one of the inner circle of President Tudjman's government, in that he was meeting regularly with other members of the government and President Tudjman during the period of Karadjordjevo, late March/April 1991?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct, and it is really surprising that he never said a word -- I apologise, that he never said a word of that at all the meetings. Ah, yes, I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: You gave us the answer. Now, it's also true, isn't it, that President Mesic and President Tudjman went back a long way? In fact, both of them served prison time together in the early 1970s as a result of the Croatian Spring incidents; isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not true. It is not true that they knew each other that well, according to my information. And as far as I know, Mesic was never in prison. Oh, well, yes, yes, it seems he was. Okay, he was, then.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: All right. Now, I want to take you to President Mesic's testimony, then, on this issue from the Blaskic case, which is now public. And we've got it in Sanction, Mr. President, the transcript's there, because I want to put some of this to the general. This is page 7136 of the transcript from the Blaskic case, starting at line 11. President Mesic said, and I'm quoting: "Tudjman, at one point, told us that he was going to go to Karadjordjevo alone -- this was on 30 March of 1991 -- that he wanted to see what they wanted." And I'm going to skip down a couple of lines where President Mesic talks about why he was against the meeting, and then on line 20 he says, quoting: "Tudjman came back from Karadjordjevo that same day, and he told us that the army was not going to attack us and that he had guarantees of Veljko Kadijevic, who was the Chief of Staff, and of Milosevic, and that it would be difficult for Bosnia to survive, and that we could get borders of the Banovina." And then I'm going to skip a couple of pages of his testimony, and I'm going to go to page 7137, line 16, where President Mesic testifies, and I'm quoting: "The Croatian public policy always proceeded from the position that Bosnia was a state and that it was unified, and that Croatia was the first to have recognised Bosnia-Herzegovina. However, in objective terms, taking into account everything that happened subsequently, when Milosevic created a Serb republic within the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina, the Croats formed the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna, which later became the Republic of Herceg-Bosna. It became clear that this did not consolidate Bosnia-Herzegovina, but, on the contrary, it undermined it, especially since, after a certain period of time, Fikret Abdic appeared on the scene and proclaimed the autonomy of and Western Bosnia, the area of Cazin, Kladusa and Bihac. "Therefore, on the one hand, we had a public expression of determination to support a unified Bosnia on the part of Croatia, whereas, in fact, we were following in Milosevic's footsteps, because of what Milosevic had done, and this was fatal precisely for the Croats, because, due to it, 850.000 Croats -- the majority of 850.000 Croats have moved from Bosnia-Herzegovina so that there are only about 350.000 left in Bosnia-Herzegovina." And so my first question to you about this testimony, General, is: Wouldn't you agree with me, sir, that President Mesic, based upon his position, who he was and where he was during the period of time here, spring of 1991, he is in a better position to know President Tudjman's policy in respect of Bosnia-Herzegovina, would you agree with me on that, in a better position than you to be know?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the assumption that Mr. Mesic said that in 1991 or 1992, or 1993, I would agree with you. However, if somebody says that in a court of law after 2000, then I can only say that the gentleman lied for political reasons because he wanted to blacken the president as much as possible, a man whom he could only look up to. At the time, Mr. Mesic was the president of the presidency of Yugoslavia and he could do things differently. This is a man -- and besides he says "us --" he says -- he says not "me" but "us." Who are the others?

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: You're not answering my question.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Isn't he in a better position to know what the policy was than you were? You didn't even know Tudjman at this period of time, spring of 1991, so isn't it true that he knows better than you what Croatian policy was when he talks about Karadjordjevo?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course he was in a better position, and because the position of Croatia was a principled position, he stuck to that policy, together with Franjo Tudjman. And then when he had to turn coats for political reasons, he turned coats. If he was a principled man, if he did not agree with the policy of Franjo Tudjman for principled reasons, he had to leave the position that he had. This is not a principled man, who only subsequently learns the truth. He knew that Franjo policies -- Tudjman's was correct, corroborated by thousands of documents that I showed, and then for purely political reasons he provides his statement as a secret witness, the president of the state. And he lies to the Croatian general public that he was the witness of the Defence. He was the witness of the Prosecution. Well, you excuse me, I'm begging your pardon.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: The next document is P00037.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: Mr. Stringer.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: I really hesitated to take the floor and to say -- to tell you, Mr. Praljak, that although, of course, your opinion should be integrated into the -- into what we have also in this transcript, and your testimony is very important; on the other hand, I really feel that since you have spoken about Mr. Mesic already on a number of occasions, that you have also to understand that here we only want to listen to you about those issues which you personally participated at, I mean, the reporting or information about those questions, when you were a party to it, so that is why when you answered the question asked by the Prosecution and by Mr. Stringer, then again I also say that you should have already answered that you were in a better position to say what was at that time the Croatian policy -- President Tudjman's policy or not. And you have already many times have, in a way, instead of answering the question, you went on to say that Mr. Mesic is a liar, et cetera, et cetera, so I believe that you, at that court, when already President Mesic's words had been included into the transcript, you have to -- you are -- you are, of course, open and there is a possibility to tell us what is your opinion about that, but you have always to have to talk about issues which are being raised either by the Defence or by the Prosecution or by the Bench. And it is what I wanted to tell you. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I am answering the questions, if it's possible to do so without concealing the truth. I was asked about something I simply said that I knew was publicly stated. Apparently Mr. Mesic, when returning from The Hague, publicly stated that he was a Defence witness. That's not correct. That's the first thing. Secondly, Judge Antonetti asked me about other 30 transcripts, many of which referred to Stipe Mesic. In none of those transcripts did Stipe Mesic say, Franjo Tudjman, you and Slobodan Milosevic tried to agree on the division of Bosnia. I don't agree with your thesis, as Judge Antonetti said, when I have minor problems or when I don't agree with Tudjman, I would say that. I had a lower-ranking position. So those are certain events that I participated in. In the 40 transcripts that were shown here, Stipe Mesic never said anything about Karadjordjevo and about Franjo Tudjman's policies. He agrees -- he's a high-ranking official and agrees with the policies pursued by the Croatia. Those are the facts, and you are free to draw your own conclusions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In a secondary fashion, let me ask this: Mr. Tudjman had many meetings. We saw the meetings. Is it true that he let everybody speak freely? It is somewhat amazing that a head of state can have hour-long meetings, as we noticed, in which everybody has their say. Was he a very liberal man, a very permissive man? Did he give everybody or anybody an opportunity to express their views, even views that were contrary to his?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Those who thought differently, who thought the opposite of what he thought, those who would sometimes babble, it's not just that he allowed them to speak, he actually asked them what they thought. This can be seen in the transcripts. These were lengthy and open discussions. Sometimes he might say, We've exhausted a subject, or, I have to go to an important meeting, and it was only on those occasions that he intervened and tried to hurry the proceedings up. Everyone else could say what they wanted, whether he agreed with it or not. You can see that in all the transcripts, the voluminous transcripts. They are so voluminous, it's really difficult when you see how much empty blabbering there is there.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: General, the next exhibit you have in front of you there, P00037, this is a presidential transcript of the 8th of June, 1991. So this is rather early, General. This is some -- in fact, this is even before you join the Croatian Army; correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: If I recall correctly, you joined the Croatian Army on the 3rd of September, 1991?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And the 8th of June here is actually about 17 days before Croatia declared its independence; is that also true? I say independence from the former SFRY.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the 25th of June is when all links were severed, after the air force bombed the presidential residence and almost killed Franjo Tudjman, so the JNA carried out bombing. They knew where Markovic was.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: I just asked you about the date is all, but thank you. So on this day, this is a session of the Supreme State Council of the Republic of Croatia. General, would you agree with me that you were not present at this meeting?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wasn't present.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Now, if you'll turn to page 5 of this document, and President Tudjman is talking about, at the top of the page in English, whether "we should discuss the manner in which to establish an alliance or break up." And then I'm skipping down a paragraph. He says: "So this is the reality that we cannot overlook. Also, gentlemen, if we opt for Croatia's independence, either within an alliance or total independence, Croatia's borders, such as they are today, are absurd, they are impossible, in the sense of administration and trade ..." And then I'm going to skip down a bit farther, two lines. He continues the next paragraph: "Therefore, from our point of view, no less than from the Serbian, there is the problem of - there is a need to find an essential solution to the problem, isn't that so, because the establishment of Bosnia, the borders of BH after World War II, are historically absurd, a resurrection of a colonial creation from the period between the 15th and the 18th century. "So we have finally reached a point where, on the level of official representatives of all Yugoslav republics, this issue is included in the agenda and it has been agreed that it should be solved. "Also, it seems that Izetbegovic, as the president of BH, realises that he is helpless as regards the Serbian movement aimed at breaking up BH. He also knows that the Croats of Herzegovina do not accept that situation." So he's going on. So would you agree with me, and maybe you don't know, General, because you weren't really involved in the government or even maybe the army at that time, that even before the breakup, the final breakup of the SFRY, the Serbs and the Herzegovinians did not accept the notion of having a unified or independent Bosnia-Herzegovina with its borders intact?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not true. That's completely false. If you would like an answer to this issue that is debated here, well, it's stated quite clearly that the partition of Bosnia and Herzegovina is something that the Serbs are working on. And the other important thing that you skipped, Mr. Stringer, is the fact of the proposal made by Alija Izetbegovic. What was his proposal with regard to Yugoslavia? It was that Bosnia and Herzegovina should --

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Excuse me.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've answered the question. I've answered it. Herzegovina wasn't against Bosnia-Herzegovina. And, well, it's not true what you have asked me about, that the Serbs and Herzegovinians wanted to change the borders of Bosnia and Herzegovina. That's incorrect.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: If President Tudjman said that, then he was incorrect; is that what you're telling us?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not what President Tudjman said here, because you can't take a sentence out of context. You need to see what the essence of the subject is. The way in which you have extracted this sentence is absurd, it's not correct, and I'm not going to answer that question. We'll either deal with the truth or -- but trying to confuse me with these sentences, that is not going to be successful. This is incorrect, and I will continue to tell you that you are not right. This is not something that Tudjman claimed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Well, then let's move to page 38 of this same transcript. The president starts talking, and this is President Tudjman, and he's talking about a proposal by Izetbegovic and Gligorov which he says is actually an attempt to preserve and somewhat bolster the 1974 constitution: "Basically, that is it ..." He goes on to say, and I'll just read it as a quote: "Serbia accepted it, but giving it its own interpretation in regard to the creating of an effective democratic federation, and they are sure not to change their position in this regard. Therefore, the solution lies in what was said there, in the partition of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and if we achieve that, then we can possibly look for a basis for an alliance of sovereign republics and states. "I think we shall achieve it because that is in the interests of Serbia and Croatia, while the Muslim component has no other exit than to accept this solution, although it will not be easy to find this solution, but essentially that is it." Now, General, this is just a couple of months after Karadjordjevo. Would you agree with me that what President Tudjman is describing here as a partition is consistent with the report and the testimony of President Mesic about the discussion at Karadjordjevo?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's not correct. It's completely false. At the time, Izetbegovic suggested that the Muslim people should remain within Yugoslavia, and he claimed that there were 6 million of them in Yugoslavia at the time, and only at that time the Croats said that they wouldn't remain in such a Yugoslavia. Izetbegovic could take the Serbs and Muslims into Yugoslavia but he couldn't take the Croats into Yugoslavia, and under such conditions the suggestion made by Izetbegovic was that Yugoslavia should be maintained, that they should join the Serbs, that they should amend the 74 -- 1974 constitution, because in that way Kosovo, Sandzak, and et cetera -- including Kosovo, Sandzak, et cetera, there would be six and a half [as interpreted] Muslims in that state, that was a good project for the Muslims, a good plan for the Muslims, but not for the Croats. And Franjo Tudjman said -- and Izetbegovic wasn't preparing for anything at the time. It was then said, If that's what is to happen, then we will have a partition in such a case, but not because of an agreement with Milosevic. Izetbegovic was trying to reach an agreement with Milosevic, not Franjo Tudjman.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Will you turn, please, to page 47.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: There is a misrepresentation in the transcript, page 70, line 13. It says that there would be six and a half Muslims in that state, and it's probably six and a half million or something like that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: On page 47, General, President Tudjman says the following. He's talking about an association, and I want to ask you about this. He says: "Therefore, from that proposal, at that meeting ...," although to be clear, I'm not suggesting that he's talking about Karadjordjevo here when he talks about "that meeting": " ... the only basis is that the starting point is the sovereignty of the republics and the association of sovereign republics, sovereign states. This starting point is acceptable. The rest is a matter for discussion, and it is true what they said. If we come to an agreement about this important contested matter between Croatia and Serbia, that is, Bosnia and Herzegovina, if we achieve realistic borders for the Republic of Croatia, and if this problem of the Serbs outside Serbia is solved so that Serbia is satisfied, then we can work on Serbia accepting such a foundation for an association which would be also acceptable to us and to others, or accepting total disassociation. "If it came to the possibility of creating such association, then there would be the matter of dispersing the federal bodies, which one would go where, what these bodies would be. In any case, it would be untenable for all of them to remain in one centre." So, first of all, General, would you agree with me that what President Tudjman's talking about here is some sort of an association based upon the fact that the former Yugoslavia doesn't exist anymore?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Here, reference is still being made to a federation that would represent something that was like the former Yugoslavia, so no one is discussing a state that wasn't composed of all the republics of the former state. Above all, it has to do with the federation of sovereign republics, and President Tudjman is quite clear about this. But as all realistic politicians, he's trying to see what the other players on the political scene are trying to do. America wants to maintain Yugoslavia, France also wants to maintain Yugoslavia, and --

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: I'm not asking you what France wanted.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, very well. But here's what Izetbegovic wants. Izetbegovic wants a special link with the Serbs, to Serbia, and he speaks about the Serbian problem in an objective way, as it's presented, as Izetbegovic presents it, and he says, Well, here's our starting point: It's a federation -- yes, I apologise, yes. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Prlic would like to say something. THE ACCUSED PRLIC: I'm not sure am I helping and to whom I'm going to help, but I think that everything is going to be in different light if just one sentence is written on page 4. This is a third chapter: "Therefore, I proposed a meeting of the presidents of Bosnia, Serbia, and Croatia, which the two of them accepted, and the other three as well." Which means that agreement was made, amongst six president of republic, that three of them had discussion, and then this discussion had actually took place in Split June the 12th. If we have this in mind, all other situation is possible to be judged from different point of view.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Well, Mr. President, I thought I -- I wanted to make it clear at the beginning I wasn't suggesting that the meeting referred to here is the meeting at Karadjordjevo that we were talking about, so I think that there is some -- it's clear from the record, at least, that when he's talking about a meeting, he's not talking about Karadjordjevo, and he's talking about discussions that took place among representatives of the various republics.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: What I'm most interested in, General, though, is, again, given the fact that as we know from what he said earlier, President Tudjman believes the border of Croatia, as it existed at that time, to be absurd, an absurd creation of the post World War II era, that in fact as part of this process by which Yugoslavia is going to dissolve, it's going to be an objective -- or he wishes to achieve, to use his word here, realistic borders, isn't that what President Tudjman wanted here, isn't that what he's saying, that as part of these negotiations, as part of these events, Croatia should strive to get borders which are greater, or more useful, or in the greater interests of Croatia than what he called the absurd borders that existed at the time?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not correct. Franjo Tudjman says if Alija Izetbegovic will take Bosnia and Herzegovina into Yugoslavia, to an enemy state that's already launched attacks, that is shelling his presidential residence, well, in such a case these borders can't be maintained. Izetbegovic can take out the Muslims, but, We won't sell out in such a context, we are a sovereign people. Franjo Tudjman always spoke about an alliance of sovereign states, and if Bosnia-Herzegovina were to be independent, if Bosnia and Herzegovina were an independent state, then the borders would not be changed in any way, but if Bosnia and Herzegovina, because the Muslims and Serbs so desired, wanted to go into Yugoslavia, to join Yugoslavia, we, the Croats, and independent people, will not agree to this. It's very simple, Mr. Stringer.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: So then, General, the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Praljak, one moment, please. Mr. Stringer's question relates to the heart of the indictment. This raises the question: Was there a plan to form a Greater Croatia? If that was the case, this should be set against Milosevic's project of a Greater Serbia, if there is such a project. There would be two such projects in that case, a Greater Croatia, a Greater Serbia, and we can see, on reading the document at page 47, that President Tudjman says as follows: "The problem of the Serbs outside Serbia must be resolved." And as he says this, I believe, but I stand to be corrected, he has the issue of the Serbs living in Croatia in mind, in Krajina. Now, if there are two projects, Tudjman's project for a Greater Croatia and Milosevic's project for a Greater Serbia, as far as you are concerned, what is left of Bosnia-Herzegovina? If these are two serious and realistic projects, what share is left for Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I've presented voluminous evidence about how Croatia conducted itself. We've seen hundreds of examples. I'll repeat this once more. Here, it says there was a suggestion made at the meeting the only starting point is that we should base ourselves on the sovereignty of republics, that should be a starting point. It should be an alliance of sovereign republics. You're forgetting the third player here, Alija Izetbegovic. Alija Izetbegovic, at a meeting in Split, but we've all forgotten what was going on there, at a meeting in Split he expressed the desire for a Muslim Bosnia and Herzegovina, and the B plan was that he should have his own territory in which he could create such a state. Croatia is a posteriori. If Izetbegovic wants his Muslim state, and he wanted such a state from the very beginning, it's just a question of how much territory he would have. And before Izetbegovic, the Serbs wanted their own Greater Serbia. So is it not possible to say, If that's what you want, well, then we'll go to the slaughter-house and you can kill us as you did in Croatia, because someone will come and say you had a plan. There was no plan. There were meetings at which there were discussions. They were open, public. You can read about them. There were proceedings in Croatia. There was a plan that has to be created through acts, through signed documents of an international kind. There are two sentences that have been misunderstood, there is one false testimony, and although there is a lot of evidence, signed documents, et cetera, we're trying to find out about a plan for a Greater Serbia [as interpreted]. What kind of Serbia? We don't even have a Croatia, so we're flogging a dead horse. We don't even have a Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Tudjman here, President Tudjman, talks about achieving realistic borders, realistic borders. Now, earlier in the transcript President Tudjman describes the existing borders as absurd. Is it your testimony, General, that in fact President Tudjman was satisfied with the borders of Croatia as they existed in June of 1991?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely, as far as Croatia is concerned. He only took account of the fact that there were 800.000 or 900.000 Croats in Bosnia-Herzegovina, an independent people, and when Yugoslavia broke up and when the idea of Bosnia and Herzegovina being broken up was supported by Izetbegovic and Milosevic, well, he was only interested in the national interests of the Croats, because that's the position they had placed him in.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: General, if you'll set this document aside, we're going to move to the next set of documents, unless the President or a member of the Trial Chamber has any questions.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, for the sake of the transcript, since my colleague Stringer interrupted the subject, on page 75, line 21 and 22, when the general spoke about plans, he didn't speak about a plan for a Greater Serbia, but he said there wasn't a plan for a Greater Croatia. So could this be corrected in the transcript so that the sentence is understandable?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Praljak, I must say I was expecting a more precise answer. I was assuming that Milosevic had the idea of forming a Greater Serbia. With this idea in mind, if we follow this through, at the time, for Milosevic, the Serbs living in Croatia were a problem, and Mr. Tudjman mentions this. Now, if we put ourselves in the shoes of Mr. Tudjman, and Mr. Stringer clearly highlighted this, he says that the borders may be a problem. In that case, did Mr. Tudjman also have the idea of a Greater Croatia in mind, and geographically speaking this would encompass Bosnia-Herzegovina, for instance? So there are two individuals that meet up with other people, and they could, and I'm deliberately using the conditional sense, could both have this idea in mind; the Greater Croatia, on the one hand, and the Greater Serbia, on the other hand. So what I would like to know is this: What would be left for Bosnia-Herzegovina, what would be left? And Mr. Izetbegovic's idea of having a republic, what would be left of that? This is what I would like to know.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I answered that question. I don't know who put it to me, but I have already answered it on one occasion. But I'll repeat the answer. That's why I'm a bit surprised by such questions. Your Honours, imagine Milosevic, who was very powerful at the time and his political plan was very clear - it had been put down on paper, it appeared in a well-known document published by their academy - on the other hand there was Franjo Tudjman who was also relatively powerful. There was no ABiH. The Muslims didn't even have rifles. They had nothing. So how long would it take to divide Bosnia and Herzegovina if there had been an agreement between Milosevic and Tudjman? And one other question. It's a question I would like to put. How long would Bosnia-Herzegovina last in 1992, in the spring of 1992, if I or someone else had reached an agreement with Mladic about the partition of Bosnia and Herzegovina? How long would the nonexistent ABiH, which was poorly armed, survived, how long would it have survived for? Everything would have been over in 24 hours. So how can one speak about an agreement of any kind between Milosevic, who had the JNA, and Franjo Tudjman, who at the time had nothing, but they'd reached an agreement, the assumption is that they'd reached an agreement, at least. The political solution would have been found within 24 hours in such a situation. A military solution would have been found if Petkovic, or myself, or Roso, had reached an agreement with Mladic. And this meeting in Split, at that meeting Izetbegovic was present. There was a plan for a Greater Bosnia and Herzegovina. Your Honours, there is the Islamic Declaration, which is a plan for a Greater Bosnia and Herzegovina, Muslim Bosnia and Herzegovina. This is a plan that exists in textual form, and there's a plan that has been written down on a Greater Serbia, but there is no Greater Croatia. All we were doing was trying to save ourselves, and -- am I going too fast? Very well, let's have a break, please, and then I'll go over this again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Praljak, you can see that on page 48 of this document - during the break, you may look at it - you can see that Mr. Tudjman, feeling that this issue is an extremely complex one, wishes to set up a working group comprising three to five people, and this working group would include the Vice-President Ramljak, Professor Sokol, Mr. Milas, Ivan Milas, Mr. Seks, I don't know who he is, and this group would seemingly be asked to look into constitutional issues, because of course this undoubtedly raises constitutional issues, and to work on a document which would be designed for confederation. Mr. Tudjman may have realised that it was much more complicated than meets the eye. Do you agree with this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I agree. An attempt is being made here to stick to the confederal concept of Yugoslavia, and Alija Izetbegovic does not agree to that. You know what this is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Right. We'll have the break now, because it is now a quarter to 6.00 and we need to have our second break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please proceed -- oh, yes, Mr. Kovacic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I believe that it was a good idea to correct a thing in the transcript in order to avoid any further confusion. On page 78, lines 11 and 12, I can see two mistakes that totally change the meaning. I believe that this is due to the fact the general was speaking really fast. The first sentence is this: [In English] "In this meeting in politic, at that meeting Mr. Izetbegovic was present." [Interpretation] I believe that the general said: [In English] "At this meeting in Split, at that meeting Izetbegovic was present." [Interpretation] And then the next sentence reads as follows: [In English] "There was a plan for a Greater Herzegovina." [Interpretation] End of quote. As far as I could hear the general, he said -- maybe the general, himself, could correct the transcript, because in the following sentence he goes on to explain, but again the explanation is not complete. Maybe he should repeat the whole chunk.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was speeding. I apologise to everybody, including Judge Prandler. I do tend to speed up. What I was going to say was this: Nothing was done behind anybody's back. All these theories were put forth publicly. They were said publicly at the meeting in Split. At that meeting, a reference was made to the cantonisation of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Some commissions were set up to discuss -- they were supposed to discuss that. There was no secret plan. Everything was publicly said, and I showed that in the book that I showed to you. There was a series of such meetings. On the 25th, there was shelling. The JNA wanted to kill Franjo Tudjman, Mesic, and Markovic. The Croatian Parliament passed the declaration on independence which was frozen at the request of the European community, and for three months after that, in the face of the aggression against Croatia, there were discussions about all that. So this is all very clear, very prescient. There was no Greater Croatia. It never occurred to anybody within the politics to think about that. And although I was not a member of the government, I, as a person that was dealing with that, I read all that very well and I knew that all very well. There you go.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] With the Trial Chamber's leave, I would like to remind General Praljak to correct the transcript. Did you talk about the Greater Herzegovina or a Greater Bosnia-Herzegovina, and who would that Greater Bosnia-Herzegovina belong to, to correct the transcript?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There were two plans that were written down. The Serbian plan was written down and was being implemented. That was the Academy's platform that we already discussed. And then what happened was the war. And then there was the Islamic Declaration which used the SDA structure to express the desire for Bosnia-Herzegovina to become an Islamic state. Those two plans were published. Croatia did not have anything even remotely close to that, nor did it behave along these lines, not in a single detail. I repeat, nothing was done behind anybody's back. Everything was subject of discussion. Alija Izetbegovic participated in all the meetings of the presidents of the presidencies of the republics, and as you've seen, there are maybe 40-plus such meetings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Stringer.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: General, you've got the next set of documents there with you, and these are also arranged in the order that we're going to talk about them. So if you could turn to the first document in your binder, which should be P00734. And, Mr. President, just for your information, the others -- this next set of documents relates largely or loosely to the issue of international armed conflict, I think, although it's safe to say that that issue is certainly not going to be limited to this set of documents. General, this is a document from the 12th of November, 1992. It appears to be over your signature. Do you recognise this as yours?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I recognise this.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And this is your letter to Ivan Cermak, who was an assistant to the -- assistant minister of defence of the Republic of Croatia. And what you're writing here is about Colonel Siljeg, and you say that he is a "colonel in the Croatian Army, kept on the records through the 115th Brigade, currently holding the position of commander of the Operative Zone North-West Herzegovina on the front-line since 1 February ..." And then you go on to talk about his salary, and you want to make sure that his salary is in alignment with the regulations of the Republic of Croatia and to pay off the outstanding amount. But, General, would you agree with me first - I don't think it's controversial - that on this day, the 12th of November, 1992, Colonel Siljeg was, in fact, the commander of the North-West Herzegovina Operation Zone of the HVO?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct, I believe that this is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And the time-frame here, 12th of November, this would be not too long after the events in Prozor and the fall of Jajce; is that also correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And when you say here that he's on the front-line since 1 February, what you're saying there is the reference to the front-line is, in fact, the front-line inside the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina; correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't confirm this. I can't confirm whether he was there from the 1st of February, 1992, whether he was on the front-line inside the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. This does not arise from this with any certainty. I don't know what he would have been doing there from the 1st of February. I suppose that he was in Croatia on the front-line. I don't know. I don't think that he could have been there as of the 1st of February, in the front-line in Bosnia-Herzegovina. There was no front-line at the time there.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] For my -- maybe just a remark. My learned friend, about the translation, I don't think this is correct. In the original text, it says "in the theatre of war from the 1st of February," and the translation of the document into English says "on the front-line." I believe that the front-line and the theatre of war are not one and the same. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: General, what's indicated here is that during the time that he was the commander of the North-West Herzegovina Operative Zone, at least in November of 1992, Colonel Siljeg was being paid by the Croatian Army. Can you confirm for us, General, that it was the Croatian Army, Republic of Croatia that continued to pay the salary of Colonel Siljeg as of this time?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that time, Siljeg obviously -- it seems that the salary did not reach him regularly, but he was supposed to be on the payroll of the Ministry of Defence of the Republic of Croatia, as a volunteer, in the theatre of war in Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: You mention the word "volunteer," and we'll come back to this. Is it true that anyone, any of the volunteers, as you put it, who came from the Republic of Croatia and fought in Bosnia-Herzegovina, that those volunteers continued to be paid by the Republic of Croatia Defence Ministry?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not every volunteer, but most of them from the Croatian Army who volunteered to defend Bosnia and Herzegovina and who hailed from the area - Siljeg is also a native of Bosnia-Herzegovina - they had the right, both Muslims and Croats, to keep the salary that they had hitherto been entitled to.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay. General, I'm going to ask you to skip one document and move to P00132. This is a document dated the 27th of January, 1993. It is from a Colonel Tomislav Kasic-Alisic. And it's attaching -- on the second page you'll see what's attached to this is a statement of the war allowances, and this appears over your signature, and so that would be my first question. General, could you recognise your signature at the bottom of the second page, which is the table of the war allowances?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct, this is my signature, and I requested -- or, rather, this was one of the groups that had gone to defend Bosnia-Herzegovina, at my request, after my propaganda activity. Could you please correct P001332? That's what I have here as the number of the document, 1332, and you said "132." There's one "3" missing, at least in my binder.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: You're correct, General, it's P01332, so you have the correct document. If I could direct you to the first page of this exhibit, which is the letter -- or the request from the colonel, and he's directing this to Mr. Susak.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I'm sorry. A remark to the transcript, which is page 84, line -- 85, first line. I think Mr. Praljak said "after my propaganda activity." Is that correct, Mr. Praljak, you said "after my propaganda activity"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, that was just one part, request and propaganda activities --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: You said that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay, General. Back to the first page of this exhibit, P01332, the letter or the request from the colonel. He's passing on your request and -- to Minister Susak, requesting that Mr. Susak approve the payment of war allowances that these people are entitled to, and he makes reference to the southern battle zone. And we'll get to it later, but I think that I recall from your testimony, you've indicated that the southern battle zone or the southern front is a reference to the area -- or an area inside Bosnia-Herzegovina where conflict was taking place between Croats and Muslims; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that's not correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Let me ask it this way, then: When you make a reference or when there's a reference to the southern front, is that a reference to a location in Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: We'll come back to that and I'll give you an opportunity to tell us what you think the southern front is. I've got more documents on the southern front, and we'll come back to that.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can do it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Now, it says here -- what the colonel is saying here is that: "We are requesting you to approve the payment of war allowances we are entitled to, as combatants, in the southern battle zone, who were sent here based on your order of the minister of defence, as it can be concluded from the attached documentation." He goes on to say: "... though we are continuously on the first front-line in Herceg-Bosna. We have been deployed there by commander of the southern battle zone, General Janko Bobetko." So, again, General, doesn't this confirm that members of the Croatian Army were present in Herceg-Bosna in January of 1993 and that they were there, as is indicated here, on an order of the minister of defence?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. First of all, they were sent on the order of the assistant minister of defence, General Slobodan Praljak. It was I who sent them, and General Bobetko received them. I repeat, it was important, very important that the volunteers who would go there to defend Bosnia-Herzegovina have -- it was a sine qua non. If they were to die there, that their families should continue enjoying all the allowances that come after their death or wounding, and that the Croatian state should guarantee that as it would to its soldiers. They were therefore volunteers. I found them through my propaganda activity. I sent them there because that's what they wanted, and now I am asking for these men to be given a salary or an allowance.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am afraid that some time has been lost in this cross-examination due to a misunderstanding between my learned friend and Mr. Praljak, due to an erroneous translation. In the original document, P1332, they were sent upon your order, the assistant minister of defence, General Slobodan Praljak, which is missing from the English. It says in the English "who were sent here based on your order of the minister of defence." [In English] "As it can be concluded ..." [Interpretation] And so on and so forth, which means that General Praljak was left out from the translation. And in the original, he is there. And it arises from the original that what Mr. Praljak said is exactly correct. "Upon my request," he said.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: I appreciate counsel's intervention. Perhaps I could just ask the general to read the first sentence of the document in the original language version.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Prlic was on his feet. THE ACCUSED PRLIC: The translation, in the document, in the Croatian language, it was written "A/A, engaged in HVO."

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. President. Sorry. THE ACCUSED PRLIC: It was allowed for me --

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Let me ask the witness to read the document so that we don't have repeated comments about what the document or the translation should or should say. Let's just read it. THE ACCUSED PRLIC: No, but it's not translated in document.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Let's just read it. If Dr. Prlic will recall, we'll ask the witness to read the document in his own language, and then we'll all take the translation together. THE ACCUSED PRLIC: No, this is not the issue, this is not the issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Stringer, I, myself, wanted to raise the issue, but Mr. Prlic asked this. I don't know whether you want to ignore that, but you know that in the B/C/S document we have handwritten "A/A," and then there is a sentence in B/C/S, and I can see "HVO" written there. It's important. And then Mr. Praljak could maybe read -- THE ACCUSED PRLIC: This sentence doesn't exist in translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And indeed the sentence was not translated into English. I've noticed that. So, Mr. Praljak, can you read out the handwritten entry?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] "Salaries in the HVO," which means that -- what's this first thing? Excuse me. "Salaries in the HVO." They should be paid for what the HVO cannot pay them, of course, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: General, why don't you just continue now to read the first typewritten sentence, just so that we can round that off.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: And I quote: "We are hereby addressing you with a request to approve the payment of war allowance which we are entitled to as combatants in the southern theatre of war, and we were sent on your order, the assistant minister of defence, General Slobodan Praljak, which arises from the documentation attached herewith." Full stop. I sent those men down there; I, Slobodan Praljak. This is my statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: General, the next question is: In the upper left-hand corner, there's a reference to a group of officers and soldiers in the 101st HV R Brigade, the letter R. Do you know what that -- what is the R Brigade?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Reserve." "R" stands for "Reserve," reserve brigades. So on the 27th of January, fighting in Croatia stopped. After the cease-fire, people were being demobilised, and I -- actually a lot of people approached me and volunteered, and I knew people from this brigade because they were in the theatre of war of Sisak for a while. I believe that some elements were even in Sunja under my command; not that I think, I know that. I knew the lads, and they were willing to go and defend Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And when they were down there fighting -- well, first let me ask the next question. When it says here, near the end, it says: "... we are continuously on the first front-line in Herceg-Bosna ..." Do you know what the location is where those soldiers were actually deployed? That first front-line, do you know the location that's referred to there?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And then the last question on this document, then: While these soldiers were down there in Herceg-Bosna, just to confirm, they remained on the payroll of the Republic of Croatia's Defence Ministry?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: This should have been the case. I don't know whether the duty was met, but it says here that one of them received monies, the allowance, and they were in Herceg-Bosna. And this is another proof that we were not dealing with any brigades. There were only 12 men, and if we have 12 men, you can't be talking about HVO brigades.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: All right. Now, we're going to move ahead about --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Praljak, look at the document you've signed, the chart where these 12 people get a monthly allocation of 60.000 dinars. Right at the top, this hasn't been translated, there are a few words or sentences in your language. Did you write this? If it wasn't you, what does this mean? It's illegible.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Truth be told, this is not my handwriting and I can't read it. I am not very good at reading other people's handwritings. With the best of will, I'm trying. Vujic signed his name. Maybe this means that he received the monies. I really can't say, Judge Antonetti, Your Honour, what this is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Mr. Stringer.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: General, we can turn to the next document, which is P01458. This is now, well, 13 days later. This is the 10th of February, 1993. Take a look at -- take a moment to look the document over, General. I don't know if you've ever seen it before or not. Do you recognise this?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a regular document, but believe me or not, I never saw it before. I was never involved in the matters of salaries, when it was due. My wife had power of attorney on my behalf to go to the bank and withdraw the money, and that's all.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: So this document indicates that as of this time, as we know, you were assistant minister of defence of the Republic of Croatia, and you were also a major-general in the Croatian Army; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: There's no doubt about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And also during this time, February 1993, now this is not too long after the events in Gornji Vakuf, you were -- let me put it to you this way: You were on the payroll -- you stayed on the payroll of the Republic of Croatia during the period of time that you were down in Bosnia-Herzegovina, say during the events at the time of the Gornji Vakuf incident?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the time of the Gornji Vakuf events, and I call it an attack launched by the ABiH, the HVO was blocked. From the 16th to the 23rd, that's when I stayed there. I was receiving my pay in the Ministry of Defence because I went there at the request of Franjo Tudjman and Alija Izetbegovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And just moving forward throughout the remainder of 1993, did you remain on the payroll of the Croatian Ministry of Defence throughout 1993, say, until the 8th of November, 1993?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Most probably, yes. I'm almost certain that that was the case, but as I never had a look at the papers, at the pay slips, to see whether the salary had arrived, I never tried to see what the Personnel Service had done, to see whether the HVO had paid. Well, I don't know, but it's most likely that the HVO paid the salary.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: All right. Now, we've just gotten an interpretation here that I want to clarify. When you -- let me just ask this: When you were commander of the HVO Main Staff, were you paid by the Republic of Croatia? Were you still on the salary or the payroll of the Republic of Croatia during the time that you were commander of the HVO Main Staff?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Most probably, yes, although as I have said, I didn't pay attention to this. I was probably receiving the same pay. But I should add that my pay was lower than the pay of soldiers in the guard. I was a civilian, that's how I was treated in the ministry and up. Our pays, well -- well, our salaries were lower than those of the soldiers. But I didn't a bit.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: So on the transcript here -- can I clarify that? If I could --

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There's obviously confusion. The same question was put, and the same answer was given, because in the transcript, page 92, line 8, it should have said Praljak said that he was receiving his salary from the HV, as far as I can remember, and then you continued with another question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Not the HV; the Ministry.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It says "the HV." Now it's clear why the question was put twice.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Actually, I'm a bit more confused now.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: General, I'm looking at line 7 of page 92, and you said: "It's most likely that the HVO paid the salary." That's what we have in the transcript, but I understood you to be saying "HV," and not "HVO."

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's correct that I was most probably being paid by the Ministry of Defence, not the HV. So my salary was lower because I was part of the civilian structure. But I'm not 100 per cent certain that at one point in time -- well, this was paid into my account, and during the war I had nothing to do with money. My wife managed, as best she could, so it's most probably the case, almost certain, that I received my salary in the Ministry of Defence of the Republic of Croatia. That's a precise answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Very well, thank you. General, the next exhibit is one of the presidential transcripts. It's Exhibit P03112. And this is a meeting of the VONS, the Defence and National Security Council of the Republic of Croatia, on the 2nd of July, 1993, with a number of individuals present, and I want to ask you some questions about this. This is jumping ahead a little bit. We were just in February of 1993 and now this is in July, the 2nd of July, 1993. So this is very shortly after the events of the 30th of June, 1993, and the attack or the offensive of the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina. And so President Tudjman opens this meeting, and one of the agenda items, and I'm looking at page 2, is "Croatian Policy Towards Bosnia-Herzegovina." And he goes on to talk about what the policy is and what the policy had been. You'll see on page 3 he's talking about some criticism that's come from others about what that policy has been. He, now on page 4 -- I'm on the top of page 4. He notes that in the ranks of the ruling HDZ, including council members, there was no unanimous support for the policy re-implemented, if you like, I'm quoting now: " ... which I implemented listening to all members of this council and others, but nevertheless I issued the decisions that I thought were in accord with the historic interests of the Croatian people and the Croatian state." And turning to page 5, Tudjman talks about how certain individuals had actually even asked President Tudjman to replace Minister Susak to limit the influence of Mate Boban's Herzegovinian Croats. Continuing on to page 6: " ... because that policy, the Croatian policy towards the Muslims, has resulted in a catastrophe and is threatening the existence of Croatia." And this is Tudjman talking about criticism of others, and then he says: "And then they conclude, both abroad and here, that there has been neither confirmation nor denial of such statements and reports." So my first question on this -- on this transcript, General, is whether you're aware of -- or were you aware at the time that there was, in fact, intense criticism even among the Croat leadership or Croat leaders in Croatia and elsewhere, whether there was intense criticism of the Tudjman policy in respect of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was aware of the fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Turn to page 50 of the transcripts, so we're going to skip quite a ways ahead, because I'm more interested in this now in terms of the discussion about how that policy is going to move forward from this point in time. At the top of page -- well, at the bottom of page 50, you see that Defence Minister Susak begins talking, and he's talking about the attitude or the views of some other countries, the Europeans, Great Britain, the United States. The top of page 2, he says: "That is why I think we must do what we must do in Bosnia and Herzegovina and, in all public statements, still speak about a unified Bosnia and Herzegovina, and all we stress, that we will do everything to protect the interests of the Croatian people there. The Croatian people there will understand this, and I think that what we are doing, what is opportune in politics." And then the discussion continues, and I want to skip over to page 54 and what President Tudjman says. He says: "All right, gentlemen, let's finish.
