"With regard to sanctions, I do not think that in such a situation they pose a serious threat. There have been, even Greguric's government, even the current government, prime ministers called me, they took steps, and at the same time my assessment was, no, I think this threat is even smaller today, but we must be careful not to give them any direct cause to serve as an excuse for their policy. Clearly, we must not do this. But at the same time we must take steps to protect Croatian interests in the territorial sense, too. And you two, please, Minister Susak, General Bobetko, see about this and meet with Herceg-Bosna leaders there, with General Praljak, Petkovic, Ambassador Sancevic, and their leaders there, with Boban and Prlic, to discuss exactly what should be done. But it goes without saying do not lead the operation in such a way as to make it a direct involvement. And what I said earlier is very important, in terms of, I don't know, a trade, of payments, I don't know what, do not let the people there feel left on their own, but let's take care in this respect." So these passages, General, where they're talking about criticism from the outside, the possibility of sanctions resulting from Croatian policy, Minister Susak here talking about doing what is opportune in politics, which I would suggest to you is an indication of a two-track policy - this is the top of page 52, top of page 52 - that what's being talked about here by Susak, and then also by President Tudjman on page 54, is a two-track policy whereas publicly things are going to be said, but in fact there is going to be, behind the scenes, activities, discussions and policies of -- Croatian policy carried out by you and others, as indicated here, which are different from what are the public statements being made in order to avoid sanctions. Would you agree with me on that?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely not. Earlier on, Gojko Susak said, and I quote, "I think that Great Britain, too, and all European countries, including the USA, are looking for any kind of excuse to identify us with each other and to impose the same sanctions on us as those imposed on the Serbs." Mr. Stringer, the policies pursued by the USA, Great Britain and France was devious. They were defending their own interests. That's what they do everywhere in the world. They presented a different truth on the HVO, the truth contrary to the facts, and they exerted the pressure. They tried to create their own truth. They tried to impose sanctions on Croatia. And Gojko Susak says, Well, look, we'll adapt, but we can't abandon what is our right. We're a constituent people, we're defending Bosnia and Herzegovina, we have spilt blood for Bosnia and Herzegovina, for an integral Bosnia and Herzegovina, but we want to defend the interests of the Croatian people within that Bosnia and Herzegovina. Since Zimmermann and the others, we're dealing with policies of force, Mr. Stringer, and that force, because it's force, isn't justice. It's not moral, it's not a matter of morality; it's not a matter of truth, either.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: So the challenge, then, was to somehow find a way to continue to exert Croatia's policy in BH, while at the same time concealing that from the internationals, the Europeans, the Americans, the British, in order to avoid the sanctions that were going to flow from the implementation of Croatia's policy in BH. You had to hide it, and that's what's being discussed here, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, Mr. Stringer, there was nothing to hide. Here, mention is made of how far we will bend our heads to satisfy the needs of force. Nothing was said about Konjic, nothing was said about the 9th of May, it was a lie, nothing about the 30th of June, so force was used to spin the truth, and we were bending our necks so much that it would hurt to please others, because someone -- what someone said from the international community was truth, regardless of what was, in fact, the truth. And that's how international policies are created. And I'm claiming here, in your presence and in the presence of the Judges, that this is not correct. And as that was the case, well, this is how it was presented for the Croatian public, too, and that's why I intervened in the Parliament, because they would sit down and then they would read out what it is said in the "Frankfurter Allgemeine Zeitung," and then they would say that's the truth. It wasn't the truth.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: So when President Tudjman says here, "Do not lead the operation in such a way as to make it a direct involvement," you don't agree with me that what he's saying there is that the work you and the others are doing, Praljak, Petkovic, for example, in Bosnia-Herzegovina, is not to be direct in a way that would give rise to international sanctions and condemnation; it has to be concealed? Isn't that what he's saying?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there was nothing to hide. What kind of direct involvement? Not even two battalions were provided. I don't know what are you talking about. You've selected four sentences here -- well, I'll go slowly.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Let me ask you this question, then, General --

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I mean, on the basis of two sentences, Mr. Stringer, we can't discuss this matter. I'd like to, but I can't answer your question, a question that involves the term "meddling," involvement. There was no involvement or meddling. At the time, there were 5.000 Mujahedin. That is meddling. What are we talking about, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Let's talk about this, then: If Croatia is not meddling, as you put it, let's talk about the role that you held down there in Bosnia and Herzegovina at this time. This is shortly before the time you took command of the Main Staff. I believe in early July 1993, you were part of the military operations in the Boksevica area; correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Boksevica, correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: But at all times, you were down in Bosnia and Herzegovina, and your job was to see to it that President Tudjman's policies were implemented and carried out; isn't that true? He was your boss. At all times, you were answerable to him, and it was your job to implement his policy; correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I was implementing the policies of the Croatian state. I wasn't there on a permanent basis. I went there at very precise points of time, often on my own initiative, not because there was an agreement with Mr. Tudjman or Susak; for example, the two months I spent in 1992 down there, well, no one authorised this. I also reached an agreement with Alija Izetbegovic. I was in contact with him. I was in contact with his adviser for military affairs. This had always to do only with peace, it had always to do only with peace and reconciliation, in Mostar and in Central Bosnia and in Vakuf and in Prozor. It was always done like this permanently, until I assumed my duties.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: All right. So that when you were in Bosnia and Herzegovina --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: "And I defended myself," interpreter's addition.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: When you were in Bosnia and Herzegovina, I'll correct myself then based on what you just said, you were there implementing policy of the Republic of Croatia, as opposed to an individual policy of President Tudjman?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was implementing the policies of Bosnia and Herzegovina, above all, when fighting the Serbs, when assisting with the refugee problem, assisting with the wounded, when it came to -- yes, very well. No, the question is too difficult. My policies were parallel to the policies of the Republic of Croatia and the policies of Franjo Tudjman, Gojko Susak, Bruno Stojic, Jadranko Prlic, and all the others.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And those were the policies that you were there implementing and trying to carry out on the ground in Bosnia-Herzegovina; correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Policies? I had work to do in the field of calming down conflicts. We don't have to use such terms, "policies." I described the events very precisely. We should adhere to the events and their purpose. When there was a meeting for weapons to be handed over for Tuzla, then there was such a meeting. When there was another meeting for weapons for Tuzla, then that was another meeting, where Croatia was to give weapons for Tuzla. When I was giving weapons for Sarajevo, and this might have involved Bruno Stojic, I might have acted on my own, but these were weapons for Sarajevo. So let's adhere to the fact. We don't have to use grand words to cover things that are incorrect.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Mr. President, I think I've finished with this document, and I can save the next one for tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Stringer, the Registrar has told me that you've already had two hours and forty-five minutes. As you all know, we will be sitting in the afternoon tomorrow. We shall meet again in this courtroom at a quarter past 2.00. I wish all and every one a pleasant evening.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
